notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1323.tmp1323.opp-lat: Ch. III: 'hoc ingens hujus omnibus domicilium' seems corrupt (perhaps 'hujus orbis'); rendered tentatively. Ch. XVI: read 'clementior' (gentler) for 'dementior'. 'Quam vero veta' read as 'quam vera'. 'Andegavae' taken as Anjou (Angers). Ch. XVIII: 'colligit' taken as 'receives'.

XXXVII: 'Sioalira' is evidently the Swale (Bede's Sualua); the form is likely corrupt. XXXVIII: 'intransvadab(??)' read as 'intransvadabile' (unfordable). XLII: the edition prints 'orbi (morbo)'; translated with 'morbo' (disease) while keeping 'world'. XLIV: Cernel is Cerne (Abbas), Dorset. XLIX: 'Veturnosus' unidentified; 'relatum (sic)' taken as handed-down report. XXX: 'angere' read as 'augere' (increase).

Scanning errors read as evident: lacrymosa (LI), tanta (LIII), mundum, crebrescentes, earum, prius, haec, et. In 2.1a 'sui mosius' appears corrupt; translated as 'animosius' (more boldly). 'centopolim (an Gigan zopolim)' is the edition's alternative reading, perhaps 'Gigantopolim'; Hebron's biblical name Kiriath-arba is meant. 'rege(??)' read as 'reges' (kings). In 2.4 'generorum' read as 'generosum'. 'Albanis' in 2.2 may refer to Alba or to Albania; uncertain.

In §5 the reign of Maurice is described as 'fifty-fourth from Augustus' (i.e. the 54th emperor). In §8 'Gregorius' is played on as 'watchful' (Greek grēgorein). In §9 'montes reges, et colles duces' is translated as it stands; it adapts Isaiah 55:12.

The chapter heading reads 'AEthelredi', evidently an error for Aethelbert, the king converted in this chapter; translated as printed. Several evident scanning errors were read silently (e.g. 'laudem' for 'tandem', 'lanium' for 'tantum', 'Borcales Auglorum' for 'Boreales Anglorum'). The Psalm quotation is cited by the edition as Ps. 58:17, but the words are those of Ps. 85:17 (Vulgate numbering) and the reference has been given accordingly. 'Andegavensem civitatem' is presumably Angers. 'Camera Cantiae' is rendered 'storehouse'; the sense is uncertain. In ch. 13 the parenthetical '(amiserant obventuras)' is an editorial supplement and the clause is obscure.

In 17, 'urgonte id nos intendite' is read as 'urgente id nos intendere'. In 18, 'quis digne memoret quam est dilata' appears defective (no subject for 'dilata'); 'his conversion' is supplied conjecturally. In 19, 'in peregrini' read as 'peregrini'; 'vulneratam clementiam' is marked (sic) by the edition and translated literally. In 20, 'ipsum Oceanum Romanis praesides exhausit' read as '...praesidiis exhausit'; the sense (stripping Britain of Roman forces) is clear but the wording is odd. In the final passage 'Na hos' read as 'Nam hos'; the deer simile ('post serpentum virus intendens') follows the bestiary belief that the deer thirsts after eating serpents.

Several scanning errors read as evident: 'Ang simus' = Augustinus; 'faciam' = faciem; 'liba mina' = libamina; 'legalis' = legatis; 'Reda' = Beda; 'a Rhoffi' read as Rhoffi (Rochester); 'ingentem magnam' = in gentem magnam; 'tuum est' for 'tuum, ... est'. 'non surgeret' follows the editor's conjecture 'non fugeret'. 'publicani' (ch. 25) seems corrupt; translated as 'the people's' (perhaps plebem/populi). 'cura loquentibus' is unclear; read as 'cum colloquentibus' ('who speak with him'), uncertain. 'litteralis' (sic) taken as 'litteralibus' (letter-bearers).

Line 28: the clause 'Sed in isto dono coelesti ... quod ... debeat formidari' lacks a main verb in this text; translated as 'there is something which ... ought to be feared'. The scripture references are given as printed in the edition; 'Joan. III, 17' should be John 5:17 and 'Joan. XIII, 5' John 13:35. Scanning errors corrected silently: 'ni I' for 'nisi', 'privato uae' for 'privato suae', 'terne' for 'terrae', 'perf uatur' for 'perfruatur'.

In 31 the edition notes a variant reading 'Deum' for 'Dei' ("champion of God"); the variant has not been translated. In 31, 'tonsure/crown of Peter' (corona Petri) refers to the monastic tonsure. Evident scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'praepo ita' = praeposita, 'corrig udo' = corrigendo, 'ret ibutorem' = retributorem, 'pes(??)lenitae' = pestilentiae).

Line 32: 'a Lucius' read as 'Lucius' (stray letter). The date 156 and 'Marcus Antoninus Verus' with 'Aurelius Commodus' follow the text as given (after Bede), though historically confused. 'Bancornhabarhe' is evidently a garbled form of Bede's Bancornaburg (Bangor-is-y-coed). 'Wicciorum' = the Hwicce. The Matthew citation is printed as XI, 39; corrected to 11:29. 'Lega Cestra' rendered Legacaestir (Chester); 'Broithmailus' is Bede's Brocmail. 'glossentur' (var. grassentur) taken as 'claimed'.

36: 'AEthercum ducem' read as 'aethereum ducem' (heavenly leader), i.e. Augustine. 'quem ut patrimum institutorem' (marked sic) is obscure; rendered 'founder of his inheritance', perhaps for 'patrium' or 'primum'. Acts reference printed as 'III, 0'; should be 3:6. 37: 'renasceremur' read as 'renascerentur'; the river name 'Sirarios' is a garbled form of the Swale ('Sioalira' earlier). 40: 'ultronea' taken as 'ultroneus' (unbidden); 'taratara' is unclear, rendered 'rattling'. 'Cyrus' read as 'Syrus'; 'Cresi' as 'Croesi'.

42: 'cura morte' read as 'cum morte'; 'dolorem [F. dotorum]' read as 'dolorum'; 'in aliis len is' is corrupt, rendered tentatively 'in other lands'. 44: 'bebraco' read as 'hebraeo'; the Latin-Hebrew etymology of Cernhel (Cerne) is the author's own. 45: 'remedia' read as 'remedio', 'petiere' as 'potiere'; 'quinquagesimus psalmus' is Psalm 50 (Vulgate numbering, Miserere).

Several evident scanning errors read as intended: medimni for medicum (47), filiis for liliis, relinere for retinere, poliicitationem for pollicitationem, ires for tres, sevo for aevo, catigeta for catechista (48). 'Scotia' here in medieval usage most likely means Ireland; King Colomannus and Bishop Monalchius are known only from the Life of Livinus. In 47 'induviis' (garments) is taken figuratively for his former afflictions; the sense is somewhat strained.

49: ‘in filios liliorum a producta longaevitate benedixit’ is obscure; the ‘a’ may be a stray footnote mark, giving ‘blessed me … with long-extended life’. ‘seminiverbium’ taken as ‘babbler’ (cf. Acts 17:18). 49: ‘sancio’ read as ‘sancto’. 50: ‘pali’ read as ‘pati’. 51: ‘Tura’ read as ‘Tum’.

Line 53: 'quod sedet saturos' read as 'sedat' (satisfies). 'dulciter' has a variant 'dulce est' (it is sweet [to recall]) noted in the edition. Stray footnote marks after 'His' and 'Hi sunt' omitted. The epitaph's 'Horum tituli... sunt hi' introduces inscriptions not printed here; the verses follow as separate lines. Line 'Laurenti sede secundus' is ambiguous (second, Laurence, in the see). 'Theodorus... fert sabbata septimus alma' plays on the seventh day; sense uncertain. 'Berta' in the last line is unidentified: perhaps an error for Bregwine or another archbishop of Canterbury buried there.

nodes.text: THE LIFE OF ST AUGUSTINE, BY GOSCELIN THE MONK.
PROLOGUE.
(From the Paris edition of Jean Mabillon.)

To the dearest lords and sons of fatherly love of the Church of St Augustine, with their reverend head of the monastery, that most abject [man], not worth remembering, yet the sincere friend of all: greeting in the Lord. I had resolved not to bring this history out of its bridal chamber, as a very beautiful daughter of the divine bride and mother Church, until, arrayed in its ornaments, headbands and necklaces, it could come forth without blemish. But since your imperious love was impatient of delay and pressed [me] more sharply, we are at last compelled to present the longed-for [daughter] in modest appearance, since we cannot do so in beautiful [appearance]: for many disturbances of affairs have taken away the elegance we intended and a swift approach [to the work]. How true the things we have written are is proved by the times, places and persons, when, where and among whom they are known to have been done; your writings too, both ancient and modern, and also the eyes of those now living, bear undeniable witness. As for our having made new things out of old, or our spreading things recently done in a recent style, let no dweller in antiquity be indignant at novelty, lest perhaps he seem indignant at God, who is always creating new things: for the God of Abraham is the God of Augustine; and he who worked the ancient signs works the same today in his modern and present-day saints, he to whom the prophet cries: Renew the signs and change the wonders (Ecclus. 36:6); he creates new heavens, and sitting on the throne makes all things new. If the ancient Fathers had not accepted what were then held to be new things, there would now be no old things for us. But the Jews and the other unbelievers, enemies of holy novelty and truth, prefer to remain in the darkness of their antiquity and error rather than be enlightened by the light of the new grace. Those too seem to imitate this even under grace itself who, weighed down by the rancour of old custom, shrink from being renewed for the better by the new miracles of God. Most men, too, refuse to believe what they scorn, and what they love they eagerly seek out and believe; but let no one despise a herald of truth, of whatever sort, or however small: for just as a lie cannot be true by anyone's authority, so truth has its own authority in itself, in anyone at all. And things commanded through a vision or in dreams are proved true by the outcome of events: as we read that the sick were bidden in sleep to come to the tombs of the saints for the sake of healing, and that, obeying, they received health there. Whoever prefers to mock this evidence of truth as idle dreams rather than heed it, may as well reject as dreamers both Joseph and Daniel and the other prophets, and Joseph himself in the Gospel, and the foreigner Nebuchadnezzar, who beheld divine mysteries. There are also those who are foolishly indignant when miracles of the saints done upon lowly persons are recounted, as though the names or memory of such people were shameful: whereas not a word is said for their sake; rather, all things are told for the sake of the glory in God of those [saints], [and of him] who does wonders in the least. For the Lord of all does not disdain to name the beggar Lazarus by name; and indeed neither Herod, nor Judas the betrayer, nor Caiaphas would be named in the Gospel, were it not for the sake of the Lord or of his own, against whom they plotted. Let kindly souls know that we set this forth because of the disputes of various people, lest along with the detractors they begin to grow weary of what they love, and to believe more weakly what they have known more truly: for evil talk corrupts good sense. We have made two books on the same matter, a greater and a lesser: so that the lesser may obligingly comply with friends from outside who are easily wearied, and the greater may overflow more richly for the sons of the house who desire it. Yet the greater has certain things, and the lesser certain things, which the two books do not both have; and the one has the savour of some seasonings, the other of others. Likewise the same deeds are told one way there and another way here, so that each needs the help and grace of the other. Of eloquent Ulysses the poet says:
He was often wont to tell the same thing differently.
Playing piously with pious friends in this and piously commending [it], we pray both those present and those to come to remember our affection and devoted service, however unwelcome.

Here ends the prologue, in which we have corrected two words by conjecture; we shall take the same liberty hereafter in what follows, but in such a way that the reading which we judge to need correction is given in square brackets. Likewise we sometimes add words lacking to complete the sense, but within (), to stand only until, after collation with other manuscripts which we have not yet been able to see, the original integrity is supplied by someone who may wish to deserve well of the saint and of this work of ours by that labour. Mabillon moved the author's division into the margin and gathered the chapter titles at the beginning. The same is kept here by numbers, with only a new division of chapters introduced, suited to our plan of keeping uniformity, as will likewise be done in the first book on the translation.
DIVISION OF CHAPTERS.

CHAPTER I. As the Lord, the victor over the world, distributes the kingdoms of the captive tyrant to his palm-bearers, Augustine, the divine legate, receives from the Roman summit the inheritance of ocean-girt Britain.
II. Here the world of Augustine is described, as a kind of earthly paradise, fruitful in all things, and pleasing.

III. The Lord prepared this vast dwelling of this world [?] for his Augustine, as he prepared the world, created from the beginning, for created man; and Augustine, leaving his homeland, was made into a great nation.
IV. Pope Gregory took him up to send in his stead to England, so that he might make the Angles, a fair people, an angelic people.
V. The man of virtues is sent, with forty Gospel companions, to convert England. They go armed for the fruitful endurance of glory.
VI. The saints, terrified by an evil rumour, are more strongly encouraged through Augustine by a letter of Gregory to the journey of virtues they had begun.
VII. The letter of the blessed Gregory to them, that they should steadfastly obey Augustine.
VIII. A letter of the same pope to Aetherius, archbishop of Arles, that he should provide what is needful for Augustine and his companions.
IX. When Augustine reports the apostolic commands to his companions, they hasten through adversity and prosperity to the true rewards, heavenly grace consoling them also with miracles.

X. In Anjou the pilgrims of God, driven out by women, follow the staff flying from Augustine's hand for three stades; resting at night under the open sky, they are lit by heavenly splendour, and are refreshed by a spring brought forth from the ground by God; and there the leader wrote his name and the reason for his journey.

XI. The neighbours, terrified at seeing such radiance by night, run to the place in the morning; finding the saints gone, they lament their guilt; from the letters written on the ground they recognise Augustine; they found a church there in his honour, which excludes every woman for ever.
XII. A matron with a candle, trying to enter it, perishes before the threshold at the very forbidden boundary, her bowels burst, and she struck all of her sex with sharper terror.

XIII. A miracle heard from the bishop of Angers himself, who dedicated this church when it was rebuilt: how at the dedication crops trampled to the ground and wholly despaired of proved more abundant than all others at harvest.
XIV. Augustine with his companions, after various dangers on land, landed in Britain, the perpetual dwelling foreordained by God.
XV. The island of Thanet was the first to receive Christ in his saints; a happy land, most happy in its fruitfulness of so many God-bearing newcomers.

XVI. Aethelbert, king of the English, third of the kings but the first worshipper of Christ, made gentler by his Christian wife, receives from Augustine the excellent message of eternal salvation; but he does not readily assent, so that glory may grow for the saints from the difficulty. He comes to Thanet to hear the newcomers, the standard-bearers and heralds of the Lord's cross.

XVII. Augustine sets out to the king the excellent message he has brought: namely, that the creator and redeemer of the world has opened the kingdom of heaven to the human race, and has made earth-born men native citizens of heaven; and that he so loved men that he willed to become man, and moreover, after countless miracles and portents of his divinity, to die by death on the cross for love of men, and that he kindled his envoys unquenchably to convert the nations, invincible against all torments; and that they themselves, spurred by such a flame of charity, had come.

XVIII. King Aethelbert indeed praises the promises of eternal blessedness, and receives the saints for their goodwill; but he does not yet know how to put off the darkness of old error and put on the new light.

XIX. By the king's clemency, or rather by God's providence, the holy newcomers, with the standard of the Lord's cross raised and with melodious prayers, entered Canterbury for a perpetual dwelling, and lived like angels, as pilgrims of the world and natives of heaven, gathering to themselves fellow heirs of the kingdom of God.

XX. In the church of the blessed Martin to the east of Canterbury, once founded by Roman Christians, the faithful guardian of the queen, the blessed bishop Liudhard, performed the divine offices, which the most holy Augustine with his choir made radiant with apostolic life and teaching, and with an abundance of signs, by which he converted many.
XXI. The king, won over by the sweet allurements of eternal happiness and the irrefutable examples of virtues, is subjected to Christ in devout faith.

XXII. The king, from most exalted made most humble, from a prince a child of the Church, is baptized in the confession and name of the supreme Trinity, is filled with the white dove of Christ, and from an old idolater becomes a new worshipper of Christ. Hence Augustine sings to God with the heavenly choir, rejoicing that his prayers have thus prospered.

XXIII. The king glories in a new brotherhood with the crowd of nobles and common people baptized with him, and no longer reckons the kingdom he governed as his own, but strives to transfer the whole of it, with the kings and peoples subject to him, into the sweet dominion of Christ and to extend it; for the bishops he builds in royal fashion monasteries and churches, like the Lord's fortresses.

XXIV. Augustine, offering himself to apostolic and ecclesiastical election, that is, to the Lord's own choosing, is consecrated by the archbishop of Arles as the first patriarch of England, and brings back a perpetual blessing to Canterbury.

XXV. Augustine sends to Rome to announce to the blessed Gregory that the king and people of the English have received the worship of Christ, that he has been made bishop, and that workers are now lacking for the great harvest. The pope sends him back the apostolic pallium and very many teachers to help, as well as answers to various questions.

XXVI. The letter of the blessed Pope Gregory on the sending of the pallium, on the rights of the bishop of London, on the metropolitan of York, and on Augustine's authority over all the priests of Britain.

XXVII. Likewise his letter to Augustine by Mellitus, that the idols be destroyed, and that well-built temples be purified with holy water for the divine offices; that the faithful should not sacrifice animals to the devil, but should kill animals for their own food to the praise of God, and give thanks to the giver of all things.

XXVIII. Likewise the pope himself, having heard of so many and such constant miracles of Augustine, as he cries out rejoicing to the glory of God, so, fearing lest the man grow proud through human weakness, he tempers the man of wonders by sending a letter.

XXIX. Likewise the blessed Gregory himself, rejoicing in the Christianity taken up by King Aethelbert, exhorts him in a sweet letter to guard this grace carefully, and to extend it more quickly to the peoples subject to him, to overturn the temples, exhorting, frightening and correcting his subjects, and to build [churches] after the example of Constantine, the most pious emperor, who cast away the idols and turned Rome with the peoples of the nations, with his whole mind, together with himself to Christ; at the same time he advises him to obey Augustine, so that God may hear him the sooner when he prays for him.

XXX. The same most excellent enlightener of the churches also graciously praises the venerable Queen Bertha in a letter, both for the king's conversion and for her devoted care for the blessed Augustine and his companions; and he urges her to increase these renowned merits more attentively.

XXXI. These honeycombs of Gregory's sweetness in his letters the blessed Augustine gathered, as he climbed the starry ladder by the steps of all the virtues; the king and queen too, drinking them in according to their devotion and capacity, strove to obey the apostolic teachings, so that after perishing kingdoms they might deserve to attain the heavenly ones.

XXXII. The Britons, the remnants left by the conquering English, who dissented from the rule of the Church, were summoned by the king's help, and Augustine strove with all the urgency of a father's love to bring them to lawful concord with all; but it is very hard to correct those who unreasonably resist reason.

XXXIII. The Lord's advocate, having called a blind man into their midst, said: "In this let the Lord of all things show whose side's teaching is true." He sets the blind man before the Britons to be healed; when they decline, Augustine gives the blind man sight with the sign of the cross. The defeated Britons ask for a delay, until they consult their people and the synod is held again.

XXXIV. The bishops of the Britons, on consulting, [are answered] that they should receive Augustine as gentle and humble of heart if he rose to meet them as they arrived, but reject him as proud and fierce if he stayed seated. They came, and indignantly rejected him as he sat and did not rise for them. He, wishing still more gently to win them, proposes three things to be kept, tolerance being given for the rest: that they should celebrate Easter at its proper time as all the Churches do, that they should perform the sacraments of baptism in the Church's order, and that, evangelizing the English together with him, they should gain brothers and fellow citizens of the kingdom of God. But when they rejected everything, he foretells that they would perish at the hands of those whom they did not wish to have saved.

XXXV. This prophecy of the Lord's herald was cruelly fulfilled by Aethelfrith, king of the English, who destroyed the Britons in war; and of their monks, who were fighting against him the more vigorously by prayer, he killed twelve hundred.

XXXVI. After the evils foretold to the incorrigible Britons, Augustine, intent on the salvation of all, goes to the metropolis of York; on the way he raises up a man disabled by paralysis and blindness, and makes him a Christian.
XXXVII. That on the day of the Lord's Nativity he baptized more than ten thousand believers, besides a countless number of children and women, in the river Swale.

XXXVIII. Where they not only crossed the unfordable depth unharmed, but all the sick also received health; where too a church has been built in memory of the blessed Augustine, and many benefits are granted to the faithful.

XXXIX. Concerning the letter of the blessed Pope Gregory sent to the holy patriarch Eulogius, in which he glories in the Lord over the conversion of the English accomplished through Augustine, and that he and those sent with him seem to imitate the powers and signs of the apostles; and about the ten thousand or more baptized in one day.

XL. Returning happily from York, he meets a sick man wasting away with the foul whiteness of leprosy, murmuring for his fatherly mercy with tearful complaint; he, with loud-crying compassion, hears together with the Lord the loud-crying desire of the silent murmur, and in the power of Him who says in the Gospel, "Be clean," by holy faith he renders this pallid man perfectly clean.

XLI. Augustine, desired by all good men and hateful only to the enemies of light, disfigures with everlasting disgrace, in the spirit of Elijah, the untameable abusers of the saints, he who continually restores suppliant sick people to health.

XLII. To this punishment is added another judgement on another people of incorrigibles: namely that, by a new disease unknown before in this world, all, from the least to the greatest, should burn with fire, until, purged of the dross of impiety, they were fused into the precious mass of faith; and the unquenchable punishment was quenched only by the baptism of Christ, with Augustine's help; and this plague is banished from this country for ever.

XLIII. Augustine and his companions, having departed from the aforementioned resisters, burn with severe thirst; but the Lord comforts their leader himself by His appearance and speech, that he should firmly believe he would obtain whatever he faithfully asked for.

XLIV. The Lord's prophet fixed his staff in the place where the fountain of life had appeared, and brought forth [a spring] abundant for the thirsty and health-giving to those with various diseases; he called the place Cernel from 'seeing God', and there founded a church to the Lord Saviour in memory of so great a revelation, where also a monastery built in honour of Peter, prince of the Apostles, stands out.

XLV. To the parish priest of Cernel, gasping towards death from disease, Augustine appears at night and orders him to go to the aforesaid spring, commonly called by his name, and there to sing the fiftieth psalm three times with a threefold washing of the body; he rises, recovers the strength to go, obeying the commands returns healthy, and in the morning performs the priestly offices for the people.
XLVI. Augustine, having travelled through part of Britain, returns to Canterbury, his perpetual dwelling, and is received with the joy of all, like the return of their sun.

XLVII. The devoted healer restores a young man condemned [to lack] walking, hearing and speech; and when he again, with his usual insolence, abused his health and was struck back with his former disability, the Father's kindness again restores him with a threefold healing.

XLVIII. It is read that he was present at the baptizing of the blessed martyr Livinus, that a heavenly splendour shone over the baptized, that the divine right hand blessed him three times with the sign of the cross; then that, by the command and guidance of an angel, he came on foot over the waves of the wide sea, as if over a flowering meadow, to Augustine, and received from him the teachings of all perfection; having kept him with him for five years, he consecrates him a priest to the Lord, and, generously endowed with priestly insignia, and made from a disciple the teacher of his own people, sends him back.

XLIX. The testimony of Veturnosus, whom his third generation, surviving to this day, asserts saw the blessed Augustine, and rose from his baptistery a modest Christian from being a slippery and most clouded [man]; and that he [Augustine], surrounded by a constant crowd, performed countless signs. The present survivor also reported, as handed down from ancient times, the holy Father's appearance and patrician bearing, [and] stature; and that, travelling through the country barefoot, he got calluses on the soles of his feet.

L. Now wholly wounded with eternal loves, now drawn from earthly tumults into the rest of the Lord, he did violence to heaven with frequent knockings of prayers, sighs and tears. At last, understanding from the answer of the Holy Spirit that his desire had been heard, he ordains with all solemn joy as his successor the blessed Laurence, renowned for apostolic virtues and foremost of his companions, while the king with the gathered people rejoiced immensely, as once Peter, prince of the Apostles, [ordained] Clement, namely because of the needs of the new instruction.

LI. Now, having sweetly exhorted the king, the Church and the people to persevere in the faith and love of Christ, and leaving to all pledges of lasting love, in the presence of the king and of bishop Laurence, amid the tearful swarms of all, with a heavenly dance surrounding him, he passes to the eternal festivals of the Lord; let us, his feeble praisers, follow him not with funeral laments but with songs of triumph.
LII. In the monastery which he founded, dedicated by Saint Laurence, the most precious pearl of his body is laid to rest with rejoicing.

LIII. How beautifully Rome, the parent of Churches, brought forth such pledges, who stand out as fathers and founders of the whole British Ocean! With what odour of sweetness and splendour of glory one love and one chamber binds together those who, distributed among the various nations of the world, each as patron to each people, shone forth like the sun.
CHAPTER ONE.
Deeds up to his arrival. Miracles performed in Gaul.

1. The most mighty conqueror of the tyrant of the world, drawing all things to himself in the judgement of the cross, bearing the insignia of the name once foretold, Swiftly strip the spoils, hasten to plunder, distributed all the spoils of the captive robber to his victorious captains: Peter seized Rome, the citadel of the world; Paul, girt for war, subdued all things; to Andrew fell Achaia, to John Asia, to Matthew Ethiopia, to Thomas and Bartholomew the vastest India, at the rising of the sun; and, not to go on at length through each, at last Gregory, the chief precentor of the Lord's wedding, embraced the circle of the earth with apostolic wings; and Augustine, for whom this crown is woven with heavenly gems, girded with his apostolate the other world of the British Ocean. Happy Rome, which, after the first princes of the contemplative faith, brought forth such princely consuls of the Church. She, once all-powerful in the Augustan monarchy, then almost submerged by the whirlwinds of wars, survived in order to beget these two great lights of the world, the one to rule the day, the other to rule the night that was to be turned into day. Gregory, among the sons of light, shone before the Christian world like the sun of the day; Augustine lit up the dark world of heathendom and the nocturnal chaos of the Ocean with a lunar lamp, and, with the dawn following, turned it into the noonday sun of Christ. This stubborn zone of the world, hedged about with the arms of nations and of demons, Augustine invades more boldly than once great-hearted Caleb [took] the city of a hundred (or the city of giants), Mount Hebron. This is your portion in Christ, this your inheritance, this your homeland transferred to heaven. O star born of Rome, and our Patriarch in this region! You won this land for the Lord; you won it for the Lord, and you yourself possessed it. Whatever of piety this land puts forth, whatever it brings to flower, whatever it brings to fruit, you are its tiller, you its sower, you its planter; all of it in the Lord is yours. Whatever saints too it has brought forth, you are their founder, their leader, their prince; all look to you, accompany you, crown you, all that you laboured for the Lord: you shall eat the labours of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you. You the kings, nobles, fathers and people follow; you they hail together as protector and first father.

2. But with what praise shall I extol this Augustinian world? It is a kind of earthly paradise for earthly men; whatever wealth is found anywhere either grows here or is brought in by the encircling Amphitrite from nations flowing in from every side. You would believe that the vast world had either found here together or stored up here the riches and delights that it bestows piecemeal in its several parts. It is an imperial kingdom, ruled in Augustan fashion by the Roman Caesars, who gloried that they had the throne of the world here as much as at Rome. The land is plentiful, fertile in all sowings and plantings, producing abundantly not only what is native to the country but even the plants of Greece or of more distant regions. It lies open very widely in most fertile fields, blossoming meadows, broad plains, rich pastures with milk-giving flocks, horses and herds for war. It is watered by thickly multiplying springs, leaping brooks, notable and famous rivers, lakes and pools ever full of fish and birds and shipping, convenient to cities and peoples. Groves and woods are in leaf, on plain and mountain, full of acorns and wild fruits, rich in game of various kinds. There are also chestnut woods, welcome at the feasts of the rich; vineyards too rival the richest fields not only of Gaul and Italy but also of Alba, Argos and Carthage. There are salt springs here, there are also hot springs, and hot rivers, built up with hot baths. What shall I say of the riches of the sea, which fill and adorn this kingdom not only with ships' merchandise but also with countless kinds of fish? Among these, various great swimming creatures are taken everywhere, dolphins and seals, and moreover mountainous whales. Shellfish glow red beyond the dyes of India and Sidon; and while elsewhere all things change or lessen their beauty with age, these keep their lustre more tenaciously, and are spoiled neither by sun nor by rain. In shells is found the value of ornaments, namely the gleaming little globes of pearls, bright with whiteness, and the many-coloured beauties of pearls.

Some are red, others green; these are clothed in purple colour, these in hyacinth, these in leek-green; but the greater number of them are white. With these the skill of goldsmiths, among choice stones, adorns the golden necklaces of the church; and even these are equalled or surpassed by the gold weaving of English maidens, who star royal and episcopal insignia, flaming with steeped purple and twice-dyed scarlet, with splendid pearls and outstanding gems set in gold, and make the precious garlands shine more brightly with their blend of craftsmanship. Pearls are produced alike, as sisters, only by Hesperia, Britain and eastern India. This land also lavishly produces the stone jet, the more precious as it is rarer in other ages; it shines with a gem-like blackness; it is also found purple, wax-coloured, whitish, green; it burns when brought to fire; when rubbed and warmed, it attracts light matter as the magnet does iron; when it is burned, serpents are put to flight. Rich masses are also dug out of veins of metals, copper, iron, lead, tin, silver and gold. You would marvel too at the lofty rocks and crags, and the temples and walls everywhere wrought laboriously from stony mountains, and adorned with a kind of native marble.

3. This vast dwelling, then, of so beautiful and rich a world the lavish hand of the Lord prepared for his beloved Augustine; he who once, when he founded the world and finished all its adornment, at last brought in man, his friend, whom he had made, and for whom he had prepared these things. So the blessed Augustine left his sweet nurse and august mother Rome, embracing instead of his homeland a long and dangerous pilgrimage, that from raging nations he might bear fruit in patience and win an everlasting inheritance for Christ. He went out from his senatorial kindred with the patriarch Abraham, and coming into the land provided by God he became a great nation. He was multiplied as the stars of heaven, in a following multitude of saints and a faithful people of nations. Rightly therefore did he grow into so many sons of love, who came to lay down his life for foreigners. Others conquered bravely; he conquered both bravely and happily, who with martial spirit bore a bloodless martyrdom. Rightly too, he who left all things both obtained the kingdom of heaven and received here all things a hundredfold; whose angelic charity and most noble generosity, most lavish to all and most sparing to himself, trampling down appetite, made this most abundant kingdom, pompous for proud emperors, beneficial to all. Happy poverty, which has enriched so many! Blessed abstinence, which ever feeds an unfailing household! By his straitening ourselves we are enlarged; by his fasting we feast; nay rather, he himself in his heirs possesses all things and is exalted. But while we write these things, this maritime Elysium has blossomed with the world growing green again, and among the Easter flowers, as the heavenly birthday of the splendid Augustine drew near, it smiled with every beauty. It is pleasing therefore to return to the course of his foretold coming, and then to recount some of his countless virtues.

4. Gregory, the distinguished lawgiver of the Lord, had seen boys for sale at Rome, charming with red-gold hair and exceptional beauty; and as he was poured out to all with the bowels of charity, he eagerly asks the names of their people, their province, and their king. He hears that the inhabitants were called Angles, the province Deira, the king Aelle; but that all were given over to paganism. The kindly soul groaned that flowers so fitting for the paradise of God were bound over to the foul altars of demons; but soon, like a prophetic interpreter, rejoicing at the omens of the names, he said: Well [are they called] Angles, shining with angelic faces; well Deirans, to be rescued from the wrath of God; well too is the king called Aelle, in whose land let alleluia be sung. He therefore set out on the journey to convert the English; but by the outcry of the Roman people, nay rather by the Spirit of the Lord Jesus providently directing all things, he was drawn back; for the Lord was reserving this grace for another friend. But when he took up the apostolate at Rome, the very thing by which he had earlier been hindered from his purpose gave him a more powerful plan: for what he could not do himself, he accomplished through his splendid lamp and armed right hand, Augustine. He found him after his own heart, the one remedy in the Lord for his holy desire, a man of all virtues, ready for the Lord's wars, eager for the crown through hard and brave deeds; like the tower of David, fortified, in which are the shield and spear and all the armour of the mighty, and fitted for all things: an evangelical vessel of the knowledge of God, a golden vessel of the Lord's election. He marvelled at the noble spirit, more eager than his own exhortation, so that he seemed not so much to wish to follow to the palm as to run ahead.

5. So, having gathered an angelic fellowship of learned heralds of Christ, who were to be companions, helpers and fellow workers in the Gospel to their leader Augustine, once he had found them all ready and of one mind for the work proposed, he offers unceasing thanks to the author of all good will. Without delay, having exhorted them most diligently and armed them for the fruitful patience of glory, with everything well [another reading: nearly] provided that befitted pilgrims in the world, he commends them to God and to the angels of peace, and sends them on the way of everlasting salvation. It is long to set out, but devout to recall, what darts of wounded love the souls, so holy and so sweet, of the blessed Gregory and Augustine and the holy brothers, torn from the motherly womb of the monastic Church, felt in their bodily separation, what prayers for a blessed reunion, what sighs, what tears they gave one another: since they did not hope to see again in this exile their beloved homeland, nay rather the faces of fathers and companions so dear to one another; and they were moving away to a barbarism so distant and so foreign, and to such uncertain perils of life. So once the cows carrying the ark of the Lord both lowed after their calves taken from them, and yet never turned aside from the straight line of the road. For the saints, going, went and wept as they passed over to the homeland of life, sowing the seeds of virtues in tears; but coming, they will come in the resurrection with rejoicing, carrying the sheaves of gladness out of grief and death. The year then was the six hundredth from the incarnation of the Lord, the fourteenth year of the reign of Maurice, fifty-fourth from Augustus, about the hundred and fiftieth year since the English had invaded Britain, and the fourth of the ordination of the blessed Pope Gregory, when he, the most illustrious jewel of the Roman pontiffs, sent to the English these starry lights, with Augustine shining before them. The soldiers of the Lord's embassy are numbered at about forty, imitating, that is, by four tens, the Law and the Gospel and the four living creatures. So many scouts the Lawgiver had once sent to view the land of promise; but those, except for two, were faithless; these were faithful; those, strange children, lied to the Lord; these, sons of adoption, clung to the truth. They went forward like sheep to the sacrifice, truly a great spectacle to the world [another reading: of the world], a sight for angels and men; terrible to the powers of the air, like an army set in array.

6. They had already gone far from their kindred house, some days' journey, eager to run the way of the Lord's commandments: but indeed, as the Truth says, The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak; and, Without me you can do nothing; they had to be taught from human weakness to act manfully, not by presuming on themselves but by hoping in God; and to conquer in him who conquered the world. In God, says the Psalmist, we shall do valiantly. So the athletes of God, forgetful of their constancy, are carried off by the empty talk of men, fanned by the deceit of demons. It is reported that the people they were seeking was more savage than beasts, that it preferred cruelty to feasting, that it thirsted for the blood of the innocent, that it abhorred the Christian faith, that it answered the teachers of salvation only with tortures and slaughter; the saints could indeed be punished without cause, but the enemies of truth could be swayed neither by reason nor by signs. Despairing therefore of the salvation of such people and of their own progress, they made their superior Augustine, who could not resist them, their envoy to the blessed Gregory, who had given him to the English as bishop, should they receive Christ; begging most humbly through him that he would release them from so dangerous and fruitless a waste of labours among unknown tongues, and grant them a peaceful return home. For such men were as yet weak, ready indeed for the Lord's campaign, but untrained, as once the Lord's disciples, willing but not able to follow him to his passion, were meanwhile hidden in a refuge until they were clothed with power from on high; but having seen the glory of his resurrection and ascension, they were so encouraged and made capable of the Spirit the Paraclete that they rejoiced more in sharing his sufferings than they feared to follow him to heaven. The charity of great-souled Gregory could then have been troubled, as at a frustrated undertaking and at the mockery of insulting demons, had he not hoped in the name of the Lord, in whom he believed his undertakings would be happily completed. Filled therefore with the spirit of power, he sends through their leader Augustine to the pilgrims of Christ this letter of fatherly exhortation, urging them both to obey him and confidently to complete the journey and the work begun, as far as the palm and crown of glory, with the help of God.

7. Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to the servants of our Lord. Since it would have been better not to begin good things than to turn back in thought from those that have been begun, it is fitting, most beloved sons, that you complete with the utmost zeal the good work which with the Lord's help you have begun. Let neither the toil nor the tongues of evil-speaking men deter you; but with all perseverance and all fervour carry through what you have begun, God being its author, knowing that greater glory of eternal reward follows great labour. And obey humbly in all things Augustine your superior, who is returning, whom we have also appointed your abbot; knowing that whatever you fulfil at his admonition will in every way profit your souls. May almighty God protect you by his grace, and grant me to see the fruit of your labour in the eternal homeland: so that, though I cannot labour with you, I may be found together with you in the joy of the reward, since I am willing to labour. May God keep you safe, most beloved sons. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourteenth year of the reign of our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, the thirteenth year after the consulship of the same our lord, in the fourteenth indiction.

8. To Aetherius, archbishop of Arles, too, Gregory, watchful for all according to his name, wrote thus, that he should provide the necessary support for Augustine and his companions, envoys of Christ to Britain: To his most reverend and most holy brother Aetherius, fellow bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God. Although among priests who have the charity pleasing to God, religious men need no one's recommendation, yet since a suitable time for writing has offered itself, we have taken care to send our letter to your fraternity, informing you that the bearer of these presents, Augustine, servant of God, of whose zeal we are certain, has been sent by us there with other servants of God for the benefit of souls, with God's help: and it is necessary that Your Holiness help him with priestly zeal and hasten to give him your support. And so that you may be readier to assist him, we have charged him to explain the matter to you in detail, knowing that once it is known you will lend yourselves with all devotion for God's sake to supporting [him], since the matter also demands it. Further, we commend in all things to your charity the priest Candidus, our common son, whom we have sent to govern the patrimony of our church. May God keep you safe, most reverend brother. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourteenth year of the reign of our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, the thirteenth year after the consulship of the same our lord, in the fourteenth indiction.

9. When Augustine, therefore, reported these apostolic instructions to his companions and pressed them more deeply, they were so strengthened that they rejoiced to run through what they had begun more boldly than they had begun it, fearlessly, and, in the manner of the best soldiers, wrested victory more fiercely after flight. So they went with the heavenly living creatures before their faces, and did not turn back when they went. Already their great-souled leader Augustine seemed to say to them with Gregory's mouth: You shall go out with gladness and be led forth with joy; for the mountains, kings, and the hills, leaders, shall leap up for you, waiting to receive you with joy. O boundless joy, by which, though through bitter and harsh ways, one goes to the endless kingdom with an unfailing wealth of merits and the sweet fruit of sons won for God! Understanding this, the saints hastened through adversity and prosperity, through level ground and thickets, to pass over to the true rewards; patient in all things, made obedient even unto death. Among so many merits of virtues, the lights of miracles always accompanied the blessed Augustine: of these countless ones, the most famous is the one which, as a pilgrim, he then showed in Anjou, a rich province of Gaul: because of it, the church consecrated in his honour never admits any woman. Hence many most honoured men of Anjou, coming to Canterbury to St Augustine, marvelled greatly that here, where he rests in the body, all women enter so lawfully and freely, whereas there none can obtain the favour of this permission. To their wonder the brothers answered that those women, namely, who drove out the saint are rightly repelled from his church; but these, who received him willingly, ought to be received by him. For long since, indeed, very many nobles and famous leaders of that people, and also reverend fathers of ecclesiastical rank in England, and above all at the shrine of Augustine himself, their patron [as they boast], are frequently celebrated as most steadfast witnesses of the things he did among them. All these by their accounts called England blessed, and above all apostolic Canterbury, in the privilege of the supreme Augustine and in his bodily presence itself, as if in his bodily life, of whom among them there was so indelible a memory, and frequent miracles, either written or more evident than writings. Here, then, let us relate from public knowledge what signs of his presence he left there.

10. Carrying out the Lord's embassy, as was noted above, he crossed from Rome with that holy band of companions, in the province of Anjou, the bridge called the Bridge of Sai [Or: Pontum], built of stonework for the length of a mile over the river Loire. When they tried to enter the neighbouring village of Sai, of the same name, the inhabitants repaid hospitality with hostility; and they drove back so many foreign men, humble in their travel on foot and in their dress, as if they were so many wolves and unknown monsters. But the women, gathered together in a crowd, raged against the saints of God with such irreverence, and indeed madness, with howling, contempt, jeering and mockery, that the men seemed in a way gentle or harmless by comparison. Nor was it enough for them to have thrown them out; they pressed on further, dragging, pushing and harassing them, driving them off with mocking persistence. Nearby stood a large and shady elm, fit for weary travellers to rest under: the saints wished to rest beneath it that night, but could not, because of the attacks of the women, as of so many dogs. One woman pressed on the Saint's heels more shamelessly than the rest, and while he raised his staff and tried to drive her off, as though fighting a beast and a ravening she-wolf, suddenly, by a new sign of God's grace, the staff flew from his hand like an arrow shot from a bow, and came to rest fixed in the ground at a distance of about three stades. Soon he followed with his blessed company [for he perceived by the divine Spirit that he was being called there at the Lord's bidding], ran up, and drew out the staff, or rather with the staff drew out the surge of a spring, which at once burst forth in an abundant flow. By this the servants of God, rendering immense thanks to their giver, were relieved from a heavy thirst and sweetly refreshed, and there that night they rested, most devout in divine praises. Then too the mercy of the Most High, unwilling that the sons of his light and of the day should suffer the harm of the bare ground at night and the open air, suddenly poured over them a light from his highest heaven, surpassing the radiance of the sun; and though they lacked a roof, he covered them that whole night with heavenly splendour, as if that very church, left under the open sky, had prayed in the prophetic words: 'Show me, Lord, a sign for good, that those who hate me may see and be confounded (Psalm 85:17); for you, Lord, have helped me and comforted me.' So all the neighbours saw so immense a ray, directed from the summit of heaven down to the saints; so that to their own confusion they might fully recognise how great citizens of heaven they had thrust out from their lodgings. And the most holy leader himself wrote thus in the ground with his staff beside that spring: 'Here Augustine, servant of the servants of God, had lodging, whom the blessed Pope Gregory sent to convert the English.'

11. Now, as the twilight of dawn approached, hastening eagerly to their appointed destination, they sped their journey through the city of Anjou [Angers]; and their despisers of the day before, now eager for them and poor amid plenty, they left empty of their saving presence, as God's zeal, no doubt, willed. In the morning, then, the neighbours ran from all sides to the place where they had seen so great a miracle of light; with heavy groaning and lamentation they sought again those who had been taken away: then, beholding the benefits of the new spring, they wasted away with sharper grief for their guilt. 'Alas, wretches that we are,' they said, 'how have we lost by our impious rejection so great a good, which we had of its own accord in our hands, and did not deserve even to be blessed by such angels!' So, learning from the aforesaid writing the longed-for name of blessed Augustine and the office of his embassy, and kindled by the frequency of the miracles, they as quickly as possible built a church beside that spring and had it consecrated in the name of blessed Augustine himself; and where the letters of his inscription were found they set up the altar; where that perpetual miracle endures, as we showed before, that no woman can ever enter that church or draw water from the spring: so that the world may know, of course, how greatly this sex offended God in the wrong done to his servants.

12. A certain illustrious matron tried to enter there with a great candle, as though the saint would now flatter her power and her gift; and to those present who tried to deter her she replied that she had not sinned against the saint, but wished to honour him: and she pressed on with her bold purpose. Scarcely had she touched the forbidden boundary and the sacred threshold when suddenly her intestines burst and the inward parts of her belly boiled out onto the ground, and the unhappy woman collapsed and died; and dragged outside dead, she taught all, terribly, to believe what she herself had not believed. By such a rebuff all women have been so instructed that they shrink from touching the doors when open even more than when shut. Yet so that the women there might not seem altogether bereft of the holy Father's grace, the inhabitants, [moved] by long-standing [Or: divine] compassion, built a suitable shelter for them before the doors of the church, where they could gather, pray, pay their offerings and vows, and take part in the sacred mysteries.

13. Now, while these things were confirmed both by ancient report and by the recent testimony of most distinguished men of Anjou, it happened that the most reverend and most prudent bishop of the people of Anjou came to his most longed-for patron Augustine, and with great devotion visited again, as it were, so ancient a guest of his homeland. He [Perhaps: This man] too was intent not only on hearing the miracles written above from the brothers, but on relating them unprompted: and he set them out in the same way in which they are written, with firm assurance, as if reading them. He also added a new miracle, as if of yesterday, made manifest in his presence, together, that is, with such favour and grace of the Father. 'O you happy ones,' he said, 'to whom the everlasting presence of blessed Augustine has fallen! Nor are we so unhappy, for whom his blessed memory has remained forever. Our homeland indeed knew him before you, and Anjou saw the wonder-worker before England did: but we, I confess, in our forefathers rejected him when present; yet, terrified by heavenly signs, we pursued him with amends as he departed: and since we no longer deserved to touch him either with hand or with sight, we began to keep him by building a church in his honour. Why should I delay your hearing of the miracle shown there with a circuit of words? As the people's devotion grew toward so great a father, always ready to hear his suppliants, always ready to grant, they began to restore more loftily that church of his reconciliation, and to bind his patronage more closely to themselves in friendship. This church, then, I dedicated in the month of May, namely on the day of the deposition of so great a father, amid the great prayers of both sexes, to the memory of him whose it had been before, while a countless multitude of people flocked together. All around rose the dense crops of the fields, now nearing harvest, now growing into ears and awns. The people, rushing in from every side like a river, paid no heed to the grain, nor to whose harvest it was. The labour of men and oxen was trampled and crushed as on a threshing floor; the hope of the fields and of the crops was ruined: indeed the fruitful straw seemed not so much beaten and crushed as a threshing floor swept and stripped. What then? All said farewell to that year's wealth, and said farewell also to Augustine, hoping that other [gains than they had lost] would come to them through his bounty. But at last, when matters were desperate, a more wonderful power [appeared], through the unfailing merits of Augustine: for so great an abundance of crops sprang up for harvest that same month over all that devastation that no land of that province could equal it, either in richness of grain or in height. Astonished by these wonders, the people rejoice to extol blessed Augustine with such praises that they believe and proclaim that he can obtain from the Lord whatever he wishes, in any nation whatever, and can grant whatever is faithfully asked.' The aforesaid bishop, publishing these things to grateful hearers with the whole country as witness, gave to all a fitting certainty of how devoutly the ancient signs are to be believed, in such new manifestations.

14. Now after Latium, after Italy, after the Gauls, after so many mountains, plains, forests and rivers, so many differences of lands and peoples, at last Augustine, the God-bearer, peace-bearer, salvation-bearer, with his blessed company, reached Britain by a happy course, namely, the abode and everlasting rest divinely preordained for him. The way of the just has been made straight, and the path of the saints prepared, and the Lord our God led them by a wondrous way to a sure place.
CHAPTER II.
Arrival in England. Conversion of the holy King Aethelred. Joy of St Gregory the Great.

15. Royal Kent has a very large and famous island, Thanet, of a size to hold six hundred households: it opens a gateway and a harbour to the throngs from overseas, a land most fertile and rich, and a fitting storehouse for Kent; the river Wantsum, three stades wide, separating it from the mainland, has made it an island: stretching both its ends into the sea, it can be forded only at its two mouths. This island, then, first received Christ in his saints, a land happy in its fertility, but most happy in giving hospitality to so many God-bearing strangers, or rather so many citizens of heaven! Here meanwhile the new father of England with his holy company is refreshed from the brine of the sea.

16. At that time King Aethelbert reigned over the English, the third of the kings of the English, but soon to be the first worshipper of Christ. By the providence of heavenly election he, presiding over other kings as well, beyond his predecessors, had extended his rule as far as the Humber, a very vast river, which divides the southern and northern peoples of the English by its flow between. To him, ruling royally in the metropolis of Canterbury, Augustine, the Lord's envoy, sent word through messengers and through the interpreters whom he had taken from neighbouring peoples overseas at blessed Gregory's urging, that he had come from Rome out of love and favour for him and his people; and that he brought him a most excellent message, most worthy of all acceptance, which with most undoubted faith promised to those who received it eternal and infinite joys, with the eternal God, for the ages of the heavenly kingdom. The king, receiving these things with a calm mind, ordered them to remain on the island where they had been received, and to be given what the needs of life required, until he had considered how to deal with them: for Christianity, shining everywhere, was already known to him, chiefly because he had as royal consort a most Christian woman from the kings of the Franks, called Bertha, whom he had obtained from her parents on that condition, that he would allow her to keep the Christian religion always inviolate with her companions. For the most holy bishop Liudhard was given to the queen as a most faithful companion and guardian, to strengthen her continually in the worship of Christ by pious counsels and examples amid the harmful customs of paganism. She, then, made the king, though still obedient to ancestral darkness, more lenient toward the worshippers of Christ; and as if he himself already worshipped Christ with half of his body, he opened the way to the bearers of Christ, until he too should enter. So the king, coming to the island on a suitable day and sitting with a gathering of his nobles in the open air, summoned Augustine with his little company to an audience: for the error of augury still deceived the king, like Nicodemus coming by night, fearing that if they came upon him under some roof, and knew any incantation or sorcery, they would overcome and lead him astray. But as far as light is from darkness, such a mind was far from these innocent and upright men: rather they raised the Lord's banners, by which to put demonic illusions to the test. So they came, not blushing, but bearing aloft the silver cross of the world's conqueror, and an image of the Lord Saviour painted beautifully and in gold on a panel. At the same time they sang litanies, by which the walls of Jericho, hostile to God, might fall; praying with contrite heart for the eternal salvation both of themselves and of those whom they had come to win for God.

17. When they had sat down at the king's command, Augustine first thundered with an evangelical voice: "We have come here, O king, for the lasting peace of you and of this whole kingdom, and we bring you, as we sent word before, the best news of everlasting joy: if you accept it, you will be blessed eternally, here and in the eternal kingdom. For the maker of the world, who is also its Redeemer, has now opened the kingdom of heaven to the human race, and has made of earthly men native citizens of heaven. For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, as the only-begotten himself testifies, for the world (John 3:16), so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life. For with such infinite love did this same Son of God love the men whom he had made that he deigned not only to become a man among men, but even to suffer death, and the death of the cross, for men. For thus it pleased his ineffable mercy to crush the devil, our captor, not in the majesty of his divinity but in the weakness of our flesh; and to snatch us, the devil's due prey, from the jaws of that most wicked tyrant by the undeserved penalty of the cross. His incarnate divinity shone forth in countless displays of mighty works, every infirmity being healed and every miracle performed: to heaven, the stars, the earth, the sea and the underworld he showed himself the God and Lord of all; he calmed the winds and the sea by his command, and trod the waves of the sea as if they were a solid plain. At last, having deigned to die as a man for men, he rose from death on the third day as God, and lit up more brightly with his own splendour the sun, which had been darkened at the death of its maker. He rose, I say, to raise us up again; he ascended into heaven, to lead us there in triumph. From there he will come as judge of all ages, to place believers in his kingdom for ever, while unbelievers are condemned. So do not judge us superstitious, most excellent ruler, because we have laboured to come from Rome into your lands for the sake of your salvation and that of your people, and to offer unknown peoples benefits as though they were unwelcome. Know, most gracious one, that we undertake this under the pressure of a need for great glory. For we desire, above every appetite and glory of the world, to have as many fellow citizens as possible in the kingdom of our God; and we strive with all our efforts to provide that those who could advance into the fellowship of the holy angels do not perish. For the kindness of our Christ, out of the inestimable sweetness of his Spirit, has poured this goodwill into all the heralds of his truth everywhere, so that, setting aside their own needs, they burn for the salvation of all peoples, and regard any nations whatever as parents and children, as brothers and kinsmen; and embracing all in the one love of God, they are eager to draw them to the endless ages of all joys and festivals. Such standard-bearers of the king, made witnesses of God by countless miracles, through swords, through fires, through beasts, through every kind of torment and death, have most invincibly subjected the world to their Saviour. Already long since Rome, already Greece, already the kings and princes of the earth, already the islands of the nations, drawn by the invitations of the prophets, rejoice with the whole earth to worship the Lord of kings and to serve him for ever, through whom and with whom they may reign everlastingly. With such affection too Gregory, the present father of all Christendom, thirsting most ardently for your salvation, would be held back by no fear of punishments or of death from coming to you, if he could (which he cannot) abandon the care of so many souls entrusted to him. Therefore he has sent us in his place, to open to you the way of eternal light and the gate of the heavenly kingdom: if, scorning demonic idols, you do not refuse to enter it through Christ, you will reign for ever in most certain faith."

18. While the salvation-bringing Augustine set out these and similar things, his assistants added a good deal, as the Lord gave [it to them], so that the king, not easily extricated from his ingrained error, answered like a sick man who favours his physicians but does not yet submit to the cure: "Fair indeed, and inviting to a kind of infinite glory, are the words and promises that you put forward; but since they are held to be new and hitherto unknown, it is not fitting for me to submit my mind to them and to abandon the rites of my ancestors, kept until now throughout all England. Yet towards your goodwill, by which you have come to us (as I see) from far away, and have striven to provide for our salvation as you know to be truer and better, we have wished to show ourselves in no way hostile, nor yet ungrateful: rather we wish to cherish you with kindly hospitality and to provide sufficiently for your livelihood; and we also permit you to win over to your faith and profession, by preaching and exhortation, whomever you can." So the king, so merciful to the Christians while still in paganism — who could fittingly recount how [his conversion] was delayed, so that out of the difficulty the crown of blessed Augustine might grow, and out of unhoped-for salvation a greater joy might be born for the Church of God?

19. So by the goodwill of the king, or rather by the providence of God, there were granted to the saints in the metropolitan city of Canterbury a fitting dwelling-place, promised allowances for their bodily sustenance, and the freedom to preach that they desired. And so the peace-bringing Augustine, approaching the city that was to be possessed, with the blessed choir of saints, bearing aloft as usual the silver cross of the Lord, the triumphal banner, with the life-giving image of the eternal king Jesus Christ himself, humbly invoked upon it the saving mercy of the Saviour; then he sweetly intoned this litany antiphon, and as the first nursing Church of the English took it up from him, he sang it with harmonious melody and devotion: "We beseech you, O Lord, in all your mercy, that your fury and your wrath be taken away from this city and from your holy house, for we have sinned." And they had rightly added "for we have sinned", since out of the love of Christ they had come to wash away the sins of others, as if their own, by teaching, prayers and tears. From then on, settled in peace not so much by the care of outsiders as by divine dispensation, they girded themselves more attentively for the harvest of the kingdom of God. They lived not only as exiles beyond the Ocean, but altogether as pilgrims of the whole world; they desired nothing of earthly, nothing of worldly allurement, so much so that you would marvel at them as born not of earth but of heaven. Pleasures, delights, riches, honours, and whatever might obstruct those going to heaven, they had cut off entirely: fasts, vigils, prayers and almsgiving they practised constantly, with chastity and all holiness. They wielded most vigorously the arms of Christ, peaceful towards virtue but warlike against the battle-lines of crimes, overcoming all faithlessness; holding out against every injury all patience as a breastplate; against dangers, against punishments, and even for bearing death itself, a most invincible constancy; towards the needy a wounded compassion; towards all men and even towards their adversaries a heartfelt love. Free and unencumbered by earthly baggage, they flew like winged creatures to the heavens; or rather, as the Apostle says, "Our citizenship is in heaven": except that they still dwelt on earth out of love for saving the peoples, in mind they already lived in heaven (Phil. 3:20).

20. Before the coming of the English, the Romans had possessed Britain for about four hundred years, that is, from the time of Gaius Caesar until the emperor Maximus, who, seizing the purple against the Augusti Gratian and Valentinian, drained the very Ocean[-girt island] of its Roman garrisons in all his wars. But the church of blessed Martin, which remained, founded long ago by those same Roman Christians, then adorned Kent; it still remains, well served by constant ministers, lying about half a stade to the east of Christ Church proper.

In this [church] the blessed bishop Liudhard, like a forerunner or doorkeeper of the apostolic envoys, first served the Christian queen with divine offices and sacraments, with his clergy, like a faithful groomsman; and as the deer, eager after the serpents' venom, thirsts for springs of water, so he, burning with the poisonous pagan rites hostile to the faith, was swept with his pupil the queen to that church as to a fountain of life, when the Roman teachers, outshining [him] as gold outshines silver, performed the things of God there. For the grace of God visited these pilgrims of Christ, solitary among foreigners, in these heavenly newcomers; it visited also his people, who were to believe through them, so that the queen not only worshipped Christ freely, but also, through such great teachers, the believing wife might save her unbelieving husband. In this oratory, then, Augustine with his choir celebrated the daily services of the Lord; and in psalms, hymns, prayers, and in the voice of the trumpet, by which the camp of the devil might perish, he raised the praises of the Lord night and day. Meanwhile a great grace of signs and of God's commandments commended such splendid merits of the saints: they could neither hide nor keep silent the imperial praises of Christ; more and more they made him resound with songs, with the thunder of preaching, and with the lightning of signs. They cured in turn all the weak and sick, whether brought to them or visited by them: indeed there was none, or hardly any, in Augustine's flock who did not abound in the grace of healing, so that they lit up the darkness of the heathen no less by miracles than by preaching. These promises of everlasting joy soothed the dull senses of men; such great lightnings struck the stubborn, as is sung to the Lord by the Psalmist: "Your lightnings lit up the world; the earth was moved and trembled" (Ps. 76:19). The fearful common people cried out: "Gods come down from their seats on high are living among men." So once too the peoples, marvelling at the Apostles of God as surpassing earthly things, said: "These are the holy gods of the earth." Nor did they lie in their error, as the Psalmist testifies: "The mighty gods of the earth are greatly exalted" (Ps. 46:10). So necks hitherto untamed lovingly bowed beneath the sweet yoke of the Lord, fertile fields received the seeds for everlasting fruits of life, very many believed, and, reborn in Christ, from foreigners they became adopted sons of God.

21. So Augustine, armour-bearer of the highest king, intent on all things, aimed the engine of salvation above all at the very highest head of the kingdom, so that, once the citadel of profanity was overthrown, he might raise up the starry citadel of holiness, and the world, made subject, might bow to the Saviour together with its king. Through the queen's urging, through the advice of envoys, through timely approaches, through the sweet enticements of eternal happiness, through every example and display of virtues, and through the prayers of the church kept watchfully before God, he strove to win him for his Redeemer; he strove, and in the Lord God he conquered and prevailed. The huge elephant of the land, the enormous whale of the sea, was caught in triumph by the apostolic net. For caught by eternal sweetness, taught by irrefutable truth, enlightened by the so holy and wonderful clarity of divine instruction, he renounced the heathenism of his forefathers together with the author of death, and of his own accord gave himself over to the author of life. "Let us too go," he said, "to the great prince of kings, to the most bountiful giver of kingdoms, not only temporal but eternal as well: and let us not be ashamed to have come at least last, we who might rightly be ashamed that, as we were first in kingship, so we were not first in faith. Let us at last follow those whom it would have befitted us to precede; above all since we seek that king who weighs not the dignity of person or rank, but the devotion of the soul."

22. Having spoken thus, he wished to lay his royalty down and bow before the servant of Christ, through whom he might be found worthy to be reborn into Christ's service and adoption. The minister of salvation, receiving him with a father's heart, urged him to wash away his former errors with abstinence, forgiveness, alms and tears, and with other pious works to come before the face of him who baptizes in the Holy Spirit. He forgave everyone, so that he might be forgiven, and by human kindnesses prepared himself for heavenly ones: prisons were opened, chains loosed, captives freed, and the poor and the guilty feasted with the king's friends. It cannot be told, nor need it be, with what joy the soul of blessed Augustine, which had so long yearned for the salvation of the people, exulted, what offerings of thanks it sacrificed to God. Now he saw his desire prospered, his land had yielded its fruit, and all the labours, pains and difficulties of his birth-pangs had brought forth for him everlasting joy, since in the king's conversion itself he was encompassing the whole Ocean with the Lord's yoke. So there dawned the day, most solemn for the Angles and the angels, on which King Aethelbert, devoted to God, having renounced the idols and the gods of his fathers, was born a Christian. There gathered not only the royal court of nobles and all Kent, but very many from all England, to see the most eminent lord of the kingdom prostrate at the feet of the newly arrived servants of Christ, and serving them in all their commands like their lowest slave; so that the man whom foreign kingdoms feared for his arms, unarmed poor men bound by a word. The church was adorned, the baptisteries decorated, the vessel of the Jordan and of the river of Paradise was consecrated. Asked by Augustine about his faith, whether he believed in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the rest that Catholic truth requires, the faithful confessor of the Lord answered to all with his whole heart and mouth, "I believe." So in this confession and in the name of the Trinity the English-born king was baptized and reborn: from an old idolater he became a new worshipper of Christ, from the black night of his world a morning lamp. Our Sylvester baptized our Constantine, with a renowned throng of dukes and nobles and a great multitude of believing people. At the voice of God's minister the heavens were opened, and the Lord Jesus poured into this his adopted son his dove, which the Father once sent from heaven to him in the Jordan, testifying that he was his Son. It came down in shining whiteness and rested upon the one received [var. the receiver] in simple purity, as upon a newborn infant. Hence the young Church, after Christ, the Lord's firstborn and only-begotten, rejoiced, embracing the newborn, to sing: "A child is born to us, a son is given to us." Thus the spirit of the Lord was directed upon our David from that day and for ever; and the wisdom of God enlightened the same man as a Solomon, as a light for his people. In the former David alone ten thousand were counted, and in our one prince broad Britain was made over to Christ. Since, then, the Saviour testifies that the angels rejoice over one sinner amended, we believe, not absurdly, that the heavenly hosts themselves, at the saving of this head, then proclaimed with harmonious jubilation: "Glory to the Lord of the world, for the kingdom of the English too has become our Lord Jesus Christ's."

23. From then on, therefore, the evangelical pupil of the saints and most vigorous helper of his teacher Augustine no longer reckoned as his own the kingdom which he governed, but as His to whom he had given himself with all his own; he longed rather to subject [himself] to Him and to extend [His rule], because He dispenses all the kingdoms of the world most justly at His will; he strove to bring the kings and peoples subject to him, not by force but by goodwill, as he had learned from his holy guides, into the sweet dominion of Christ. So great too was the love in the holy and God-beloved king that he no longer reckoned those who believed in the Redeemer as dependants, but bound them to himself with great rejoicing and affection as brothers and everlasting fellow-citizens of the kingdom of God. Then he generously and royally built bishoprics and monasteries everywhere, like the Lord's castles, by which the Lord's kingdom might be held. In his metropolis he most helpfully marked out a basilica of the Saviour, for his Augustine to build and possess. In its suburb he raised up a royal and apostolic monastery, to keep the bodies of bishops and kings until the day of the life-giving resurrection. He also founded a suffragan [see] at Rochester and a pontifical hierarchy in London, and churches and monasteries in other suitable places.

24. Before all else, however, he pressed, together with the whole country, that Augustine, already most choicely elected by the supreme pope Gregory, be consecrated as his apostle. And he, who at such peril of pilgrimage had sought the salvation of so many, for whom he would not have shrunk from death, did not refuse to take on the chief labour. He crossed the sea to Aetherius, archbishop of Arles, to be ordained by him, obeying, that is, the apostolic election and the church's petition, or rather the Lord's calling. Gregory's letters too had gone before him, ever most watchful on his behalf and on behalf of the beloved English. Here, then, the first patriarch of England was consecrated, and with the apostolic insignia he returned to his inheritance for its everlasting blessing, and was enthroned in the see prepared for him at Canterbury.

25. Then indeed, amid all his cares for teaching the peoples, he counted it a crime of sloth if he delayed to announce such great joys of the Lord's gain to the soul of blessed Gregory, held in suspense by holy longing. So there was sent to Rome the most holy Laurence, then a priest, afterwards the excellent successor of blessed Augustine, and Peter, a monk worthy of a monastery's headship, who later shone as the first abbot of Augustine's monastery; so that this messenger of mutual rejoicing might also grow weightily into many fruits.
