Augustine, who was rejoicing in a great harvest, complained anxiously of the fewness of labourers; to this end he consulted the divine master on various questions, how he might reform a wavering church and an untaught people. But Gregory, a man of holy desires, when he learned that the king of Britain had been consecrated to Christ with his realm, that the hands of the baptizers were failing before the peoples flocking together in crowds, that for the fertile fields only husbandmen and seed were scarce, that the people's hunger for hearing the word of the Lord needed many teachers: who could worthily relate with what joy he blessed the Most High, with what ardour of mind and voice he prayed that these increases of gladness might be strengthened for ever? "You, Lord," he said, "author of the salvation of all, you, wonderful and glorious in your saints and in all your mercies, we, frail praisers, magnify through all things. For see, through your humble envoy Augustine the Ocean, once swollen, now lies beneath the feet of the saints and serves; and the barbarous tongue of Britain has now begun to resound the Hebrew alleluia in your praises. Receive, sower of benefits, the fruits of everlasting grace which you planted in his most fruitful breast; receive your stranger and orphan with his brothers who speak with him, with whom, leaving home, country and kindred, denying himself and taking up the cross, he followed you. You are able to multiply him too into a great nation, after your ancient hearer the patriarch; and it is yours, Lord, always to temper all the difficulties and hardships of your saints, and to turn them into an infinite gain of joys." Offering these affections of fatherly love to God like incense, the most holy pope went on to pray the Lord of the harvest to direct his counsel, as to which suitable labourers he should send into his harvest. So, by the inspiration of heavenly providence, there were sent, with the aforementioned envoys Laurence and Peter, men outstanding in virtues, Mellitus, Justus, Paulinus and Rufinianus, as four heralds of the Gospels. With them went no untrained band of evangelical ministers and fellow-workers, to plunder the camps of the demons with a terrible battle-line. For whatever seemed suitable for the worship and ministry of the church, in sacred vessels, in altar furnishings, in church ornaments, in priestly vestments, in precious relics of the holy apostles and martyrs, in very many books, in every elegance of divine things, the vigilance of Gregory gathered together entirely and entrusted to these distinguished bearers of his letters. In addition he sent clearly set out answers to the questions and enquiries sent ahead, which, deferred or passed over here, you will find in full in Bede. Over and above all these was added this letter of apostolic privilege.

26. To his most reverend and most holy brother and fellow-bishop Augustine, Gregory, servant of the servants of God (Book XII, Letter 15). Although it is certain that unspeakable rewards of the eternal kingdom are reserved for those who labour for almighty God, it is nevertheless necessary for us to bestow on them the benefits of honours, so that, as a result of this reward, they may be willing to toil more abundantly in their zeal for spiritual work. And since the new church of the English has been brought to the grace of almighty God, by the bounty of that same Lord and by your labour, we grant you the use of the pallium in it for the celebration of the solemnities of the mass only, on condition that you ordain twelve bishops in their several places, who shall be subject to your authority, so that the bishop of the city of London must always in future be consecrated by his own synod, and receive the pallium of honour from this holy and apostolic see, which by God's authority I serve. To the city of York, however, we wish you to send a bishop whom you yourself judge fit to be ordained, on this condition only: that if that city, with the neighbouring places, receives the Word of God, he too shall ordain twelve bishops and enjoy the honour of a metropolitan; for we intend, with the Lord's favour, to grant him too the pallium, if life is granted him; yet we wish him to be subject to the direction of your fraternity. After your death, however, he is to preside over the bishops whom he has ordained in such a way that he is in no way subject to the authority of the bishop of London. In future let there be this distinction of honour between the bishops of the cities of London and York, that he who has been ordained first shall be held the senior. But let them arrange with one mind, by common counsel and concordant action, whatever is to be done out of zeal for Christ; let them judge rightly, and carry out what they have judged without disagreeing with one another. Your fraternity, however, shall have subject to you, by the authority of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, not only those bishops whom you have ordained, nor only those who have been ordained by the bishop of York, but also all the priests of Britain, so that from the words and life of your holiness they may learn the pattern both of right belief and of good living, and, carrying out their office in faith and conduct, may attain to the heavenly kingdom when the Lord wills. May God keep you safe, most reverend brother. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the nineteenth year of the reign of our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, the eighteenth year after the consulship of the same lord, in the fourth indiction.

27. The Lord's company, laden with apostolic riches, had already gone far on its way, but Gregory's mind did not cease to follow them as they went, for infinite love does not know how to end its services (Book IX, Letter 71). Again he renewed his singular cares for his Augustine, again for his English; and so he sent this letter also to the venerable Mellitus mentioned above. To his most beloved son Mellitus, abbot, Gregory, servant of the servants of God. Since the departure of our community which is with you, we have been left in great suspense, because we have happened to hear nothing of the success of your journey. When, therefore, almighty God has brought you to that most reverend man our brother Bishop Augustine, tell him what I have long been considering, as I pondered the matter of the English: namely, that the temples of the idols among that people should by no means be destroyed, but that the idols themselves that are in them should be destroyed; let holy water be sprinkled in those temples, let altars be built, and let relics be placed [there]. For if those temples are well built, it is necessary that they be converted from the worship of demons to the service of the true God, so that, when that people sees that its temples are not destroyed, it may put away error from its heart, and, knowing and worshipping the true God, may gather more readily at the places to which it is accustomed. And since they are accustomed to kill many oxen in sacrifice to demons, some solemnity should be given them in exchange for this as well: so that on the day of dedication, or on the feasts of the holy martyrs whose relics are placed there, they may make themselves huts of tree branches around those churches which have been converted from temples, and celebrate the solemnity with religious feasting; and may no longer sacrifice animals to the devil, but kill animals for their own eating to the praise of God, and give thanks to the Giver of all for their fill; so that, while some outward joys are kept for them, they may more easily be able to consent to inward joys. For there is no doubt that it is impossible to cut away everything at once from hard minds, since he too who strives to climb to the highest place rises by steps or paces, not by leaps. So the Lord made Himself known to the people of Israel in Egypt, yet He kept for them in His own worship the practice of sacrifices which they used to offer to the devil, commanding them to sacrifice animals in sacrifice to Him; so that, changing their hearts, they might give up one part of the sacrifice and keep another, so that, although the animals were the same as they had been accustomed to offer, yet in sacrificing them to the true God and not to idols, they were no longer the same sacrifices. It is necessary, therefore, that your Love say these things to the aforesaid brother, so that he, being present there now, may weigh how he ought to arrange everything. May God keep you safe, most beloved son. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the nineteenth year of the reign of our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, the eighteenth year after the consulship of the same lord, in the fourth indiction.
CHAPTER III.
Miracles performed. Letters of St Gregory the pope. Dealings with the Christian Britons.

28. Then also, having heard of so many and such continual miracles of blessed Augustine, just as he cried out rejoicing in the praise of God, so, fearing lest he grow proud through human weakness, he tempered him with this letter (Book IX, Letter 58): "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will, because the grain of wheat, falling into the earth, has died, so that He might not reign alone in heaven: He by whose death we live, by whose weakness we are made strong, by whose passion we are freed from suffering, by whose love we seek in Britain brothers whom we did not know, by whose gift we have found those whom we sought without knowing them. But who could suffice to tell how great a joy has arisen here in the hearts of all the faithful, because the nation of the English, through the working of the Almighty's grace and the labour of your fraternity, has had the darkness of errors driven out and been flooded with the light of the holy faith; because with a wholly sound mind it now tramples on the idols to which it was formerly subject in mad fear; because it bows down to almighty God with a pure heart; because it is restrained from the lapses of wicked deeds by the rule of holy preaching; because it submits in spirit to the divine commands and is raised up in understanding; because it humbles itself to the ground in prayer, so as not to lie on the ground in mind? Whose work is this, if not His who says: 'My Father works until now, and I work' (John 3:17)? He, to show that He converts the world not by the wisdom of men but by His own power, chose unlettered men as the preachers He sent into the world; and He does the same now, since He has deigned to work mighty things among the English nation through the weak. But in this heavenly gift, dearest brother, there is something which, together with great joy, ought to be most greatly feared. For I know that almighty God, through your Love, has shown great miracles in the nation which He willed to be chosen; so it is necessary that you should both rejoice with fear and fear with rejoicing over this same heavenly gift: rejoice, that is, because the souls of the English are drawn by outward miracles to inward grace; but fear, lest amid the signs that are done the weak mind lift itself up in presumption, and, through the very thing by which it is exalted in honour outwardly, it fall inwardly through vainglory. For we ought to remember that when the disciples, returning with joy from preaching, said to their heavenly Master, 'Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name', they at once heard: 'Do not rejoice over this, but rather rejoice that your names are written in heaven' (Luke 10:17). For those who rejoiced over miracles had set their minds on a private and temporal joy; but they are called back from private to common, from temporal to eternal joy, when it is said to them: 'Rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven.' For not all the elect work miracles, yet the names of all of them are kept written in heaven. For the disciples of the Truth ought to have no joy except in that good which they have in common with all, and in which their joy has no end. It remains, therefore, dearest brother, that amid the things which you do outwardly through God's working, you should always judge yourself inwardly with precision, and understand with precision both who you yourself are and how great is the grace in that nation, for whose conversion you have received even the gift of working signs. And if you ever remember that you have offended against our Creator, whether in word or in deed, always call these things back to memory, so that the memory of guilt may press down the rising glory of the heart; and whatever you receive or have received in the working of signs, count these gifts as given not to you but to those for whose salvation they have been conferred on you. There comes to my mind, as I consider these things, what happened to one servant of God, even one outstandingly chosen. Certainly, when Moses was leading the people of God out of Egypt, he worked wonderful signs in Egypt, as your fraternity knows. On Mount Sinai, fasting forty days and nights, he received the tables of the law; amid lightning and thunder, while all the people were terrified, he alone was joined in the service of almighty God, even in familiar converse; he opened the Red Sea, he had a pillar of cloud as guide on the way, he brought down manna from heaven for the hungry people, and by a miracle in the desert he supplied meat to those who craved it, to excessive fullness; but when, in a time of thirst, they had come to the rock, he lost confidence, and doubted that he could bring water out of it, which at the Lord's command he then opened in abundant streams. And how many things he did after this in the desert over thirty-eight years, who could suffice to recount or to investigate? Whenever a doubtful matter troubled his mind, he would return to the tabernacle and inquire of the Lord in secret, and at once be instructed about it by God speaking. He appeased the Lord when He was angry with the people by the intervention of his prayer; those who rose in pride and broke away in discord the chasm of the opening earth swallowed up; he crushed enemies with victories, he showed signs to his own people; but when they had at last come to the land of promise, he was called up the mountain and heard of the fault which, as I said, he had committed thirty-eight years before, in that he doubted about bringing out the water; and he learned that because of this he could not enter the land of promise. In this we must consider how much the judgement of almighty God is to be feared, who worked so many signs through that servant, yet still kept his fault in mind for so long a time. If, therefore, dearest brother, we recognise that even he, whom we know to have been especially chosen by the Almighty, died for a fault after signs, with what fear ought we to tremble, who do not yet know whether we are chosen? And what should I say of the miracles of the reprobate, when your fraternity knows well what the Truth says in the Gospel: 'Many will come on that day, saying to me: Lord, in your name we prophesied, and in your name we cast out demons, and in your name we did many mighty works; but I tell them: I do not know who you are; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity' (Matthew 7)? The mind, then, must be strongly held down amid signs and miracles, lest perhaps it seek its own glory in them and exult in the private joy of its own exaltation. For through signs the gain of souls is to be sought, and the glory of Him by whose power those very signs are performed. But the Lord has shown us one sign in which we may both greatly rejoice and recognise the glory of election in ourselves, saying: 'By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another' (John 13:5). This sign the prophet sought when he said: 'Make with me, Lord, a sign for good, that those who hate me may see and be confounded' (Psalm 85:17). I say these things because I wish to lay low the mind of my hearer in humility. But let your humility have its own confidence; for I, a sinner, hold with most certain hope that through the grace of our almighty Creator and Redeemer, God the Lord Jesus Christ, your sins are already forgiven. And you have been chosen for this, that through you the sins of others may be forgiven; nor will you have grief over any guilt hereafter, you who strive to make joy in heaven over the conversion of many. For our same Maker and Redeemer, speaking of the repentance of man, says: 'So, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine just who will have no need of penance' (Luke 15:7). And if there is great joy in heaven over one penitent, what joy do we believe has arisen over so great a people, turned from its error, which, coming to the faith, has condemned by penance the evils it did? In this joy of heaven and of the angels, then, let us repeat those very words of the angels with which we began; let us say, then, let us all say: 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.'"

29. The same pope, rejoicing also in King Aethelbert's nourishing faith, wrote in this form, with holy gifts: "Almighty God brings all good men to the government of peoples for this reason: that through them He may bestow the gifts of His mercy on all over whom they have been set. We have learned that this has happened in the nation of the English, over which your Glory has been set for this purpose, that through the good things granted to you heavenly benefits might also be bestowed on the nation subject to you. And therefore, glorious son, guard with careful mind the grace which you have received from God. Hasten to spread the Christian faith among the peoples subject to you. Multiply the zeal of your uprightness in their conversion. Suppress the worship of idols, overthrow the buildings of the temples. Build up the morals of your subjects in great purity of life by exhorting, by frightening, by coaxing, by correcting, and by showing examples of good works, so that you may find Him as your rewarder in heaven whose name and knowledge you have spread abroad on earth. For He whose honour you seek and maintain among the nations will also make the name of your Glory more glorious to posterity. For so Constantine, once a most pious emperor, calling the Roman state back from the perverse worship of idols, subjected it together with himself to almighty God our Lord Jesus Christ, and turned himself with all his mind, together with the peoples subject to him, to Him. Hence it came about that this man surpassed the fame of the ancient princes by his praises, and excelled his predecessors in reputation as much as he excelled them in good works. And now, therefore, let your Glory hasten to pour the knowledge of the one God, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, into the kings and peoples subject to you, so that you may surpass the ancient kings of your nation in praise and merit; and the more you wipe away the sins of others in your subjects, the more secure you may also be concerning your own sins before the terrible judgement of almighty God. As for our most reverend brother Augustine, trained in the rule of a monastery, filled with knowledge of holy Scripture, endowed with good works by God's grace: whatever he urges upon you, listen to gladly, carry out devoutly, and keep carefully in memory; for if you listen to him in what he speaks on behalf of almighty God, the same almighty God will the more quickly hear him when he prays for you. But if (God forbid) you set his words aside, how will almighty God be able to hear him on your behalf, whom you neglect to hear on God's behalf? With all your mind, then, bind yourself to him in the fervour of faith, and assist his efforts with the strength which the Godhead has granted you, so that He whose faith you cause to be received and kept in your kingdom may make you a sharer in His own kingdom. Moreover, we wish your Glory to know that, as we learn in holy Scripture from the words of the almighty Lord, the end of the present world is already near, and the kingdom of the saints is to come, which can never be ended by any end. As this end of the world approaches, many things are at hand which were not before: namely, many changes in the air, and terrors from heaven, and storms contrary to the order of the seasons, wars, famines, plagues, earthquakes in various places. Yet not all of these will come in our days, but they will follow after our days. So if you learn that any of these things are happening in your land, do not let your mind be troubled in any way; for these signs of the end of the age are sent ahead for this reason, that we should be careful for our souls, watchful for the hour of death, and be found prepared in good deeds for the Judge who is to come. I have said these things now, glorious son, in few words, so that when the Christian faith has grown in your kingdom, our speech with you may also grow fuller; and it may please [me] to speak the more amply, the more the joys over the perfect conversion of your nation multiply in my mind. I have sent small gifts, which will not be small to you, since you receive them with the blessing of the blessed apostle Peter. So may almighty God perfect in you His grace which He has begun, and lengthen your life here through the course of many years, and after long times receive you into the company of the heavenly homeland. May heavenly grace keep your Excellency safe, lord son. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the nineteenth year of the reign of our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, the eighteenth year after the consulship of the same lord, in the fourth indiction."

30. Likewise the most excellent illuminator of churches himself graciously praises the venerable queen Bertha in the following letter, both for the king's conversion and for her own care towards blessed Augustine and his companions, and he urges her to increase these renowned merits more attentively (Book I, letter 59): "Whoever desires to gain the glory of the heavenly kingdom after earthly power ought to labour more strenuously to make gain for his Creator, so that he may ascend by the steps of his works to what he desires, as we rejoice that you have done. For our most beloved son Laurence the priest and Peter the monk, on their return, have reported how your Glory has behaved towards our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine, and how much comfort and what charity you have bestowed on him; and we have blessed almighty God, who has graciously deigned to reserve the conversion of the English nation for your reward. For just as through Helena of memorable memory, mother of the most pious emperor Constantine, He kindled the hearts of the Romans to the Christian faith, so we trust that through the zeal of your Glory His mercy is at work in the English nation. And indeed you ought long ago, by the good of your prudence, being truly Christian, to have inclined the mind of our glorious son, your husband, to follow the faith which you practise, for the salvation of his kingdom and his soul, so that from him and through him, from the conversion of the whole nation, a fitting reward might arise for you in the joys of heaven. For since, as we have said, your Glory is both fortified by right faith and instructed in letters, this ought to have been neither slow nor difficult for you. And since, God willing, the time is now suitable, act so that, with divine grace cooperating, you may make good with increase what has been neglected. Therefore strengthen the mind of your glorious husband in love of the Christian faith by constant exhortation; let your solicitude pour into him an increase of love for God, and so kindle his mind also for the fullest conversion of the nation subject to him, that you may offer a great sacrifice to almighty God by the zeal of your devotion, and that the things which have been told of you may both grow and be proved true in every way. For your good deeds have reached not only the Romans, who have prayed the more earnestly for your life, but also various places, and even Constantinople, to the most serene prince. Therefore, just as joy has been given us by the comfort of your Christianity, so also may there be joy among the angels in heaven over your perfected work. So devote yourself devoutly and with all your strength to helping the aforesaid most reverend brother and our fellow bishop, and the servants of God whom we have sent there, in the conversion of your nation, so that you may both reign happily here with our glorious son, your husband, and after long spans of years may also gain the joys of the life to come, which knows no end. And we pray almighty God that He may kindle the heart of your Glory to do the things we have spoken of by His grace, and may grant you the fruit of eternal reward for work pleasing to Him."

31. With what pious avidity the yearning ardour of Augustine drank in these honey-flowing combs of flower-bearing Gregory, these nourishments of apostolic and Roman suckling, my poor understanding is not able either to grasp or to set out. In this divine armour of fatherly letters the long-proven champion of God delighted himself; in this most limpid mirror, before the eyes of his most gracious King, he examined his beauty and his adornments; on this balance he weighed what tipped down and what was in excess of his worth. And since his holy conscience answered to so many praises of virtues, he laid up everything, for the increase of graces, in the bosom of the Giver of good things; nor did he fear to be overwhelmed by his own triumph, since he leaned not on himself but on his Maker. He did not fear a fall, he whom the holy fear of the Lord had possessed, whom, founded upon the firm rock, neither glory nor disgrace could bend, who stood not in himself but in the Lord; and he imitated, for unending glory, not Peter slipping through presumption but Peter steadfast through faith, and Paul glorying in his infirmities for the sake of Christ's power. Lastly, what should he boast of, who had crushed every form of boasting, who sought poverty and lowliness instead of glory, whose building's foundations were sunk to so great a depth of humility and made firm by their masses that, while his tower, built of pure gold and every precious stone, rose up to heaven, it laughed unmoved and unharmed at the blows of all storms? King Aethelbert too responded to the apostolic exhortations of the supreme Gregory as much as he knew himself, redeemed in Christ, to be a debtor of graces, because from eternal perdition he had been made a son of God's adoption. Had he not been held supremely necessary, through royal power, for the spreading of Christ's kingdom, we believe he would have preferred to serve under monastic rules rather than to rule, and to set the crown of Peter before the crown of the kingdom. But what was not then allowed to be done in office is now clear to have been in his intention. Nor should the devotion of Bertha, most Christian queen, be passed over, whom so great a pope likewise judged worthy of the favour and commendation of the letter set out above. For she was a door open to the light, through which the splendid groomsman of the Lord, Augustine, poured Christ, the true Sun, into the inner chambers of the king's mind.

32. Since, then, this friend of God was the most faithful key-bearer of the king's heart (the heart, that is, of that king whose heart was in the hand of the Lord), with charity poured out and mind enlarged he extended his affection to the salvation of all, and he urged that most obedient prince to have the bishops of the Britons, who were straying from the Church's rule, come to a conference with him. For this land was anciently named after these Britons, before the Angles, and it had long ago been initiated into Christ. Indeed, in the one hundred and fifty-sixth year of the incarnate Word, when Marcus Antoninus Verus, fourteenth from Augustus, was reigning with his brother Aurelius Commodus, the king of these Britons, Lucius, humbly asked by letter of Saint Eleutherius, then pope, and gladly obtained, that he would send faithful teachers to regenerate him and his nation in Christ. Nor did the Britons fall away from the integrity of the faith they had received until the storm of the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, in which many were crowned with martyrdom.

But afterwards too they persevered in the Lord's faith, so much so that they did not yield to the Pelagian heresy, but through bishops of the Gauls whom they summoned they refuted the faithless enemies and drove them away. Yet at length, corrupted by luxury and arrogance, since they preferred to be subject to vices rather than to the Lord's yoke, they were destroyed by the sword of the heathen, and, driven with a few survivors from almost the whole land, they were confined to wooded and barren places. Wishing, therefore, to heal them, and to make them and the Angles one nation and one body of Christ, the Lord's apostolic legate Augustine called together the more distinguished men of the nation and began to press them with every persuasion of fatherly sweetness and with all the bowels of charity, that, renouncing every dissension hostile to Christ, they should admit the God of peace, and together with him gain for God sons of adoption and for themselves co-heirs of the heavenly kingdom. He urged them also with earnest prayers and warnings to celebrate the Lord's Easter at its proper time by the common usage and agreement of the whole world, abandoning, that is, the error by which they kept this feast from the fourteenth moon to the twentieth, in which cycle eighty-four years are reckoned; besides this, they were asked to come to their senses in many other things in which they strayed from the Church's rule. But the more gently the Britons were asked, the more fiercely they resisted; and since they claimed that their observances were superior to all others, they were bent by no reasonable restraint. They gave authority to their ceremonies, as having been prescribed not only by Saint Eleutherius the pope, their first founder, from almost the very infancy of the Church, but as having been kept until now by their holy fathers, friends of God and followers of the apostles; and these they ought not to change on account of new teachers of doctrine. What the wisdom of the most learned Augustine answered to this, let a discerning, not an obstinate, mind gather: "Your holy fathers, had they found these apostolic decrees which we bring, now accepted by the whole world, to be holier, would have obeyed of their own accord and corrected their ignorance and irregular observances; otherwise they would appear not holy but rebels against holiness. And indeed the apostles of the Lord, at the beginning of the faith, practised this one work everywhere: to teach all nations to believe in the Saviour of the world and to hope for eternal life in Him. So, not with mortal arms but in all patience and by the proofs of signs and holy works, they subjected the whole world to the footsteps of Christ. Meanwhile they could not publicly hand down lunar cycles, lest they obscure the heavenly promises with earthly concerns and, the cross of Christ being made void, should have run in vain. Few or scarcely any then disputed about Easter, especially since the rage of the whole world was punishing every soul that believed in Christ. But when kings and tyrants had been subjected to Christ and the Church began to reign, then councils were held publicly and apostolic decrees were sought concerning Easter and the other sacraments of the Church; and the things that had earlier been neglected, or were done in different ways in different places, whatever was required for the integrity of the one faith, was shaped on the anvil of the one Church. Let whoever does not wish to be cut off from Christ, therefore, share in this regular unity of Christendom." To all this the Britons strove to object rather than to agree. I could hardly believe that God's herald Augustine was ever wearied by greater evasion of words from any of the pagans: so true is it that nothing is crueller than an enemy at home or unreason among fellow citizens; for this is to fight with beasts, or to endure civil war.

33. But the Lord's follower, taught after Christ and the apostles to conquer by patience, endeavoured to try everything, so that those who resisted the Lord's embassy might at least yield to divine judgement. "Let us ask," he said, "to be taught by the God of peace and truth, who makes those of one mind to dwell in a house, through the proof of a clear sign, whose view is holier and what line is to be held in this controversy. Seek the test of truth in some sick or infirm person, who, brought before us, may prove in the name of the Lord the claim of the one who cures him to be true." When all approved this proposal, the rebels themselves too, though unwilling, a certain man of the Angles was brought to hand, in whose eyes the joys of light had been extinguished. I believe it was by God's will that an Englishman was found, lest the Britons, if he were one of their own, should swell with pride. The blind man to be cured, then, was first presented to their priests, so that when they failed, the true witness of the truth and the true physician might shine forth. So, all rashness having been confounded, Augustine bent his knees on the ground, praying his most proven hearer and the most illustrious enlightener of the world to restore sight to the blind man, so that the hearts of many might be enlightened in faith and spiritual grace. Then, placing the sign of the cross on the man with this word of faith, "By this sign let the Lord of all things show whose teaching is true," the blind man's eyelids were opened, he received light, and after long night was flooded with clear day. Praise was shouted to the Lord by all the people, and Augustine was celebrated as God's faithful witness and the truthful upholder of true doctrine. Even the Britons themselves, unable to strive against so great a light, now gave their support, and testified that his preaching, declared by so great a sign, was true; but [said] that they could not cast off their ancestral laws without the counsel and assent of their elders. Hence a respite was asked and granted until the synod should be held again and, with more people assembled, what was to be followed might be discussed. These things are recorded as done in the place which to this day in the English tongue is called Augustineac, that is, Augustine's Oak, on the border of the Hwicce and the West Saxons, where the greatest province of the Britons adjoins.

34. So seven bishops of the Britons, with many most learned men, most of them from their most noble monastery, which in English is called Bancornaburg, over which the abbot Dinoot then presided, being about to go to the council, went to a certain man renowned among them for the life of an anchorite, a holy and prudent man, and consulted him on the matter, whether by following Augustine's teaching they should renounce their ancestral observances. He said to them: "If you have recognised him as a servant of God, follow him." "But how," they said, "shall we recognise this?" Then he said: "Hear and learn from the Lord, who commands: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart (Matthew 11:29). From a meek and humble heart, then, it will be recognisable to you that Augustine bears the Lord's yoke and condescends to those who bear it. But if he displays fierceness or obstinacy, how will it be established that he is a man of God or from God?" And when they asked for an example of how to discern this, he said: "Let him enter the synod first; if he rises to meet you as you arrive, obey him reverently as a servant of God; but if, remaining seated, he scorns to receive you with the honour due to colleagues, though you are more numerous, let him also be contemptible to you."

35. Girded with these arms to their own destruction, when they came before him they found Augustine seated in the bishop's chair and not rising to them at all. Then indeed anger, indignation, contempt, rejection, quarrels and disputes bristled up, and the barbarous fury could not be softened by any gentleness of the father; not only would they not bear to listen to him, but they even tried to rebut and refute all his preaching. The man of the Lord, still striving in every way to win them, proposed, out of the many things in which they opposed the universal Church, three to be observed, so that the other differences might be tolerated: namely, that they should celebrate Easter at its proper time like all the Churches, that they should perform the sacrament of baptism according to the Church's order, and that, by evangelising the Angles together with him, they should gain brothers and fellow citizens of the kingdom of God. But the opponents rejected everything, and declared not only that they would not obey his commands or requests, but that they would not even have him as bishop. "For he who disdained to rise for us when we arrived," they said, "how much more will he oppress us if we submit to his authority?" It is clear, then, with how meek and humble a heart that faithful and prudent vicar of the Lord, who sat, bore the yoke of Christ; and with how stiff a neck and swollen a heart those who stood revealed themselves as rebels against the Lord's yoke. For a man of God is recognised not by sitting or rising, but by gentleness and brotherly love, since one may be found both most merciful when sitting and most savage when standing. Moreover, it would have been held unbecoming to the Church's sanctity that by rising he should puff up men so fierce and in error, whom he ought rather to correct by rebuke. At length the Lord's armour-bearer, brandishing the sword of the Lord over the incorrigible, pronounced this sentence with prophetic spirit and mouth: "If you will not heed one who warns, believe one who threatens: those whom you refuse to have as peaceable brothers you will have as most savage enemies; and those to whom you begrudge fellowship in the kingdom of God, by them, warring you down, you will be taken from this life and from that kingdom." So the rebels against the truth at last experienced a truth-speaking prophet. For at a later time, when Augustine had already been taken up to the Lord, the mighty king of the Angles, Aethelfrith, invaded with a huge force the City of Legions, which is called Legacaestir by the Angles, but more correctly Carlegion by the Britons. A great gathering of the Britons, both priests and monks, had assembled there to pray against the king's attack; and from the monastery of Bangor there was so great a number that, divided into seven companies, there were no fewer than three hundred men in any part, all of whom lived by the labour of their hands; their total was reckoned at more than two thousand. All these were fighting against the enemy with the arms of prayer and a three-day fast. When the king saw them drawn up in a safer place and considered the reason, he said: "Ah! These men fight against us with unarmed hand but armed prayer, and stir up their God against us more bitterly than any battle. Soldiers, break up this more dangerous line first, and destroy it to the last man." Their defender was one named Brocmail, who fled as the enemy charged and exposed to the swords the unarmed men he had been left to defend. Of those who prayed, twelve hundred are said to have been slain and only fifty to have escaped by flight; then the just severity of the victor destroyed the rest of the forces of that faithless army. Thus the perverse felt in their punishment that Augustine, long after he had triumphed over the stars, had spoken truly, whose prophecy they had despised while he was still in the body: namely, that they would be warred down by the English as enemies, with whom they would not have peace as brothers in Christ.
CHAPTER IV.
Preaching and conversion throughout the kingdom. Various miracles.

36. So when that prophet of truth had foretold these evils to the implacable Britons, he set out for the city of York, as one concerned for all. His whole journey was as busy as any stay, so that everywhere he might prepare for the Lord a straight way and a perfected people. He always went on foot, without a carriage; patient of labours, like a true follower of the holy apostles, he had taken nothing of worldly desire with him on this road of the world. Free and unencumbered, he ran along the paths of God's commandments towards heavenly things, drawing following companies with him. Communities of holy brothers, with a crowd of believers, surrounded their heavenly leader as his escort; and the further he went, the larger his following grew, as fire gains strength by moving. For who would not hasten breathlessly to join such holy companies, which desired nothing of the world except the salvation of men, even of those who persecuted them, and to such sure promises of heavenly joys? To these, credibility was given both by the examples of holy living, by the divine grace of signs, and by a unanimity ready to die for the truth. Near the borders of York, then, beside the road along which the Lord's sower of the word was travelling, there lay a man paralysed in his whole body, deprived even of the light of his eyes, and a beggar. At the noise of the people passing by he asked and learned who led the way, and he is said to have cried out repeatedly to the saint: "Holy Augustine, by the bounty of your famous kindness, help this man, who lacks both goods and health." At this the most merciful father, remembering the Lord healing the blind man in the Gospel, approached the sick man; and in the words of Peter, the Lord's key-bearer, whom he imitated with all devotion as the founder of his inheritance, he said: "Silver and gold I have none, but what I have I give you; rise up healthy in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 3:6)." Scarcely had he spoken when the sick man, who until then could not move himself, was cured by the great power of the word and leapt up; and at the same moment, as his eyelids sprang open, he drank in the bright day. And believing gratefully in the Saviour whom Augustine taught, together with full vigour of body he received the happier salvation of the soul.

37. Thus the Lord's herald, both on the way and in the city of York and wherever he came, confirmed what he thundered in teaching with manifold flashes of signs. Rejoicing in his success, like those who rejoice at the harvest, and as victors exult when the spoil is taken, he gained abundant peoples for Christ on every side; so much so that on that day of the Lord's Nativity, celebrated by the harmonies of all the heavens, more than ten thousand of the English, besides an endless number of little children and women, were reborn in the bath of holy baptism in the river which in English is called the Swale, as though by a single birth from the one womb of the Church. At the command of their divine teacher, as at the voice of an angel calling from heaven, all of them alike, two by two, entered the threatening depth of the river as if it were solid ground; and there, in true faith and confession of the supreme Trinity, they baptised one another, each by the other, while the apostolic leader blessed the water. O how great a festival! How great a joy! How delightful a spectacle for citizens of heaven and of earth! when the bosom of that most capacious channel seemed not to suffice for so great a multitude, and a generation of so many troops and companies was poured out as if one offspring from the womb of one parent, and so great a progeny was born into heaven from the depth of the stream! With what lights of the newborn did the day and glory of Christ's Nativity then shine for all those being born! With what gladness all God's angels, who rejoice over one sinner who repents, then exulted over so great a sprouting of the divine harvest, singing at the birth of the Saviour: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.

38. With all these, that is, with the citizens on high, the most blessed Pope Gregory so rejoiced in the Holy Spirit that he sent a letter about so splendid a number of believers to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, a holy friend of God, so that he too might rejoice with him. This joy is further heightened by a splendid miracle: in so great a press of crowds rushing in, with such differences of sex and age and of the sick, though all crossed through that unfordable depth, absolutely no one perished, no one complained of being crushed or hurt; but the hand of the Lord carried all, reborn in Christ and coming up from the washing like flocks of shorn sheep, across to the further bank, so that all had one birthday, both Christ's and their own in Christ. I have said too little in saying that no one was hurt there: all the sick laid down in the water the afflictions of their bodies as well as of their souls; and with the health of both the inner and the outer man, like the people of Israel out of the Red Sea or from the midst of the Jordan, an army clad in white went forth with heavenly rejoicing. There still stands in that same place a church founded and dedicated in the honour and name of this illustrious baptiser Augustine, which, by healing frequent crowds, gives most famous evidence of so great a salvation. And from the above-mentioned letter of Pope Gregory to Eulogius we add the following for the sake of credibility (Book VII, letter 30).

39. "We give thanks to the almighty Lord, because we see fulfilled in you what is written: Where there are many crops, there the strength of the oxen is manifest. For if the strong ox had not drawn the plough of the tongue through the soil of the hearers' hearts, so great a crop of believers would never have sprung up. And since I know that you rejoice with others in the good things that they do, I repay your kindness in kind and announce news not unlike yours. For while the nation of the English, set in a corner of the world, remained until now faithless in the worship of wood and stones, it pleased me, with the help of your prayer, that I should, God being the author, send to it for preaching a monk of my monastery, Augustine, a religious man and worthy of God. He, with leave given by me, was made bishop by the bishops of the Germanies, and with their support too was brought to that nation at the end of the world. And already letters have reached us about his safety and his work, that either he himself or those sent with him shine among that nation with such great miracles that they seem to imitate the powers of the apostles in the signs they display. Moreover, at the solemnity of the Lord's Nativity which passed in this first indiction, more than ten thousand English were reported by this same brother and fellow bishop of ours to have been baptised. I have told this so that you may know what you are doing by speaking among the people of Alexandria, and what you are doing by praying at the ends of the world. For your prayers are in the place where you are not, while your holy works are shown in the place where you are." From what the same honey-tongued pope wrote to the bishops of the Franks we also extract these few words: "As fire grows greater when the wind blows, so the endeavours of a good mind advance through commendation. Since, then, by the cooperating grace of our Redeemer, so great a multitude of the English nation is being converted to the grace of the Christian faith that our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine declares that those who are with him cannot suffice to carry out this work in various places, we have arranged to send some monks to him, with our most beloved common sons Laurence the priest and Mellitus the abbot (Book IX, letter 52). And therefore let your fraternity show them the charity that is fitting." How sweet it would be to rehearse what he also urged in grateful letters to Lothar, king of the Franks, about receiving the saints, and to Queen Brunhild about their miracles known everywhere, and with eager hand to gather so many pearls and honeycombs! But one must defer to the hearer who is either idle or easily wearied, since most of these things are found in the register of the most blessed Pope Gregory himself.

40. So, to take up again the journey described above: at length Augustine, the Lord's evangelist, going out from York with a company of holy companions and constant miracles, met a certain leper, disfigured by ulcerous and festering foulness. The wretch, unbidden, called out with pitiable complaints to Augustine, the bearer of salvation. Why did I say "called out"? The pestilent disease had taken away his voice; he had a hiss for speech and a rattling for a cry. The kindly healer needed no one to point him out, the most compassionate one of mercy needed no long entreaty; he felt the distress of the sick man whom he saw, and the love of Christ urged him to work health for the afflicted. Why should we delay his swift generosity with roundabout words? The diseased man came up as a suppliant, and the bishop, lavish with blessing, blessed him; and so, quickened by the presence of Christ, he said: "In the name of the Lord Saviour, be cleansed from all the filth of your leprosy." He spoke, and at once all the misery of the putrid humour fled like a cloud; and clean skin, the uncleanness wholly swallowed up, clothed the whole man. Naaman the Syrian was not cleansed so quickly, whom the healer Elisha had first ordered to wash seven times in the Jordan. But Augustine, by the word of him who said in the Gospel, "Be cleansed," prevailed in speed (Mark 1:41). O blessed and rich poverty in Christ of the apostolic preacher, richer than all the wealth of the earth! O most opulent treasure, from which is poured out not gold for greedy mortals but, beyond comparison with gold, the free salvation of souls and bodies! Could the boundless wealth of Croesus or Darius buy health for the sick? So at so great a sign the cry of the marvelling people was raised to heaven, and from every side they ran together to life-giving baptism.

41. Having worked thus on his journey, the Lord's merchant turned aside from the northern region into the western, behaving less like a traveller than like a hunter or fowler; not so much hurrying to his own home as seeking the Lord's gains, and spreading his nets wherever a divine catch might come. When he had reached the province called Dorset, and was everywhere received like an angel of the Lord, and was at the same time fed by the faith of the hearers whom he fed, he came upon a certain village as if upon the Tartarean seat of Pluto. There an impious people, blinded by their own darkness and hating the divine light, not only could not bear to hear the life-giving teachings, but, raging against the saints of God with a whole storm of mockery and insult, drove them far off from all their land; and their unbridled insolence is believed not to have held back its hands either. But the messenger of God, according to the Lord's command and the example of the apostles, shaking off even the dust of his feet against them, cast upon those savage people a sentence worthy of their deserts (not with the wish of one who curses, for he desired the salvation of all, but by divine judgement and after the pattern of Elijah), so that it might reprove with due punishment, both in themselves and in all their descendants, the despisers of the saints who had rejected the commandments of life. The story is that these men, who deserved to be struck by lightning, hung the tails of sea fish, hanging down, on the saints; and that they thereby brought forth eternal glory for the saints, but turned back lasting disgrace upon themselves, so that this shame should be imputed to a degenerate stock, not to an innocent and noble homeland.

42. Here it seems that an instance of chastisement should next be attached, which the salvation-bringing Augustine is related to have worked at that time among another nation of unbelievers. That people too, embodied with demons by long-standing profanity, out of love of darkness hating the friends of light, who in their unbelief would say to God, "Depart from us, we do not want the knowledge of your ways, we have made a pact with death" (Isa. 28:15), not only rejected the angelic teacher, who proved true doctrine by angelic conduct and by the lightning-strokes of signs, but were even burning either to cut down with swords, or to burn alive with fire, the bearers of life. Whatever the kindly preacher promised to believers, they spat out; whatever he threatened in prophetic manner, they sneered at. What then should that soul, beloved of God and labouring for the salvation of all, which would have given itself even for such as these in everlasting charity, do among people so desperate? And what will be impossible to so great a faith, and what invincible to so strong a love? So, fleeing to the inexhaustible mercy of Christ, he prays that he would break with a rod of iron, like a potter's vessel, that pot of worldly wantonness and devilish worship, such as the prophet saw boiling from the face of the North; or that he would refine that lump in his furnace for the better, and redeem by chastisement those worthy of perdition (Jer. 1). At once that whole conspiracy of the perverse is seized by an unheard-of punishment, so that affliction alone might give understanding to their hearing. All burn with an invisible fire; not sweltering as with quartan fevers or other fiery diseases, but (wonderful to tell and marvellous to see!) with the skin burnt away and the flesh turning raw, bloody feet and eaten-away thighs were displayed. In that whole raging people, as there was no one who came to his senses, so there was no one who escaped. Age and sex, the old and the suckling, parents and children, were all struck by one sentence of punishment: everywhere a clamour, groaning, and howling of torment was raised. Then at last the transgressors, returning to their hearts, understood what the prophetic Augustine had threatened them with when they despised the heavenly promises. Gathered together, they run to him whom they had spurned, they flee for refuge to him whom they had driven away; mourning, they fall at the feet of him whose prayers and warnings they had laughed at; they beg for the saving washing which they had fought against; and, the burning of punishment changed into the ardour of faith, all implore to be reborn in Christ. This is the change of the right hand of the Most High; nor can they any longer disbelieve Augustine when he promises that in baptism they would be regenerated to health of mind and body. So there is a vast festival for the heaven-born and the earth-born, when so many thousands of the reborn are joined to the citizens on high; and so that this rejoicing may shine more serenely, the cloud of sorrows wiped away, that pestilent fire devouring the rotting flesh, unquenchable by any waters, incurable by any arts, is extinguished by baptism alone, through Augustine's intercession, in all who were baptised there. From that day too this plague, which sometimes rages in other lands, has been banished from this whole country under Augustine's patronage. Those freedmen of God could then gratefully cry out: "Unless the Lord had freed us through Augustine, or Augustine through the Lord, we would have been like Sodom or Gomorrah, or would deservedly have perished by the fires of Elijah along with the enemy fifties."

43. From this digression on a similar fury and its just chastisement, then, to take up again the earlier road to be travelled: God's most holy couriers, Augustine and his companions, having gone five miles from their above-mentioned abusers through lonely places in a desert and waterless land, sat down under the open sky, worn out by severe thirst and heat. The one hope of safety for the dying men was in God and the merits of their Augustine. He, anxious not so much for himself as for the brothers, took refuge with them all in prayer to his beneficent Lord, always proven in every petition. So, as he prayed, the Lord Jesus, feeling compassion for his martyr (for a mind ready for martyrdom makes a martyr even without suffering, and his martyrdom was patient and kindly conduct among persecutors), deigned in his ineffable mercy to show himself here, and consoled him with familiar address thus: "Take strength, my good and faithful servant, and act manfully, for I, the Lord your God, am with you in all your doing; and my ears are open to your prayers, so that you may always obtain whatever you ask for, for whomever it be. For the gate of eternal life lies open to you, where you will rejoice with me without end." Blessed Augustine, drinking in such great gifts of the Lord's vision and address with the whole fervour of his heart, forgot his bodily thirst and thirsted more and more for the sweetness he had tasted; and as he had met it gratefully with his tears when it came, so he followed it with more abundant weeping as it departed.

44. Worshipping there, and perceiving that the heavenly benefits of the Lord overflowed on the place where his feet had stood, and that the ground on which the fountain of life had appeared could not suffer dryness, he at once fixed his travelling staff there. Without delay a most pure spring leapt up as if from a struck vein, which refreshed them all abundantly and gladdened them as much by the miracle as by the relief; and thenceforth for ever, drawn off into streams and brooks, it has made these places habitable and very populous. The divine father himself, possessed of so blessed a vision, in eternal memory of so great a grace, named the place Cernhel from seeing God. This name, made up from Latin and Hebrew (for as the first syllable, from cernere, means 'seen', so the following one, hel, means 'God'), has become indelibly rooted in it. For this reason too a church is built and consecrated in the name of the Lord Saviour, because he deigned to reveal himself there; and afterwards a monastery, long since raised high in honour of blessed Peter the apostle with buildings and wealth, flourishes at present with a distinguished community of monks. That sacred spring is famed under the name of Augustine its steward, offering not only the use of its water to those who drink, but also a remedy for various diseases to those who believe: of which we here give a proof by a miracle done lately, which is very famous there and widely throughout the province.

45. The most learned abbot of Cernel has a parish priest who is accustomed to perform the divine offices for the people in the monastery itself. Sickness, having brought him to the point of death, compelled him to ask for the monastic habit. The garment of holy profession was placed on his head, though he took refuge in it only then, when death was upon him; that is, he took up the armour of God only when the enemy was attacking. It was night, and sleep was overtaking the exhausted sick man. Kindly Augustine stands by the frightened man, conspicuous in his very habit and pontifical staff. Nor does he long deny a remedy to such a man, who was perhaps still living with a worldly mind; he invites him to the fullness of the prize, he who administers his sun to the grateful and ungrateful alike, and often calls back the estranged by kindness rather than punishment. The holy comforter revives the anxious man with these words: "Rise," he said, "and go to the spring of Saint Augustine, and there chant the fiftieth psalm three times over, and calling on the help of Augustine himself, wash your body three times in that same spring: so you will obtain the life and health you desire. And lest you be hindered by any doubt, know that he through whom you are to recover is himself present to you and urging this." At this the dying man rises, and seizing a staff, goes out while all marvel. To those watching over him it then seemed that he was wandering about thus as a presage of imminent death; yet they prefer to follow and observe where he was going rather than prevent him. Coming to the sacred spring, he washes three times in its stream, three times the fiftieth psalm is sung, with Augustine's aid implored; and before the offering of prayers was complete, the sick man marvels to find himself recalled from death by sudden health. Indeed, what the ancient [Elisha] had done with a sevenfold washing in the leper, our Elisha, confessor of the supreme Trinity, showed in the dying man by the threefold form of baptism. So returning to his bed, no longer sick but wholly sound, he rested sweetly; and at the very dawn of light he went to the monastery and sang matins for the people as usual. Great amazement and ecstasy seized the abbot and brothers and people, with joy and an outpouring of thanks, that they should see the man whose funeral they were waiting to perform, eager and unharmed, carrying out his usual office. He also explained to the people publicly how he had been healed so swiftly through Saint Augustine.

46. So then Augustine, the angelic envoy of the Lord, to bring his journey to an end, after long stretches of land and after travelling through a great part of Britain, after countless saving comforts of miracles and teachings, returns with that most blessed company of companions to his permanent see and dwelling, Canterbury, where, as the father and light-bringer of all, and as the most longed-for return of their sun, he is received with the favour and joy of all.

47. Among the crowds thronging to so powerful a healer of the infirm there came a young man, propping himself on his knees instead of his feet, being twisted by a severe contraction of both feet, and at the same time bereft of hearing and speech. Only for his eyes was the way open, but his misshapen gait denied him the way; he saw what he would seek, but the tongue that might speak for him had failed him in seeking it. Being mute, he kept silent about his straits; being deaf, he did not hear what it would help him to know. Whether I should call one who lacked so many functions of life half-alive or half-dead, his condition was pitiable. But the compassionate Augustine released this misery by devout prayer, and by the grace of the Trinity drove off the threefold affliction with a threefold cure. His steps are straightened, his tongue is loosed, his ears are opened; the man sick in three ways rejoices in health in three ways. He walks, runs, speaks, hears, without stumbling, plainly, clearly. Yet the slippery fellow abused the soundness he had received with such vanity and insolence that Augustine seemed to have done violence to God in asking that so undisciplined a man be granted health. For, to say nothing of the other base acts of his frivolity and buffoonery, when he came to church he affected the people with such chatter and wantonness that he scandalised them all by his shamelessness, since he neither showed reverence to the holy place nor yielded to anyone's rebuke. So divine punishment bound the intemperate man more heavily than with his former bonds, and, taking away the health that was turning to the ruin of the untamed man, tamed him by putting back on him, with greater pain, his former garments: that is, the mouth of the fool bubbling over with folly, and the ears intent on idle tales and all wantonness, and the feet too, running to the precipice, it shut with a brazen key and twisted back to restraint. So, constrained by sharper torments, he is dragged by friends and kinsmen to the heavenly physician; and clinging to the saint's footsteps, what he could not with his blocked words he bewails with dreadful sighs. Weeping and wailing he begs pardon; presuming on his mercy, he asks again for the health he did not deserve. The fatherly heart is wounded more deeply by another's misery, and mercy wrestles with the judge of mercy, by which alone compassionate justice is wont to be overcome. Between the guilty man and God the advocate stands as mediator: on the one side he rebukes him as deserving punishment, on the other he strives for his salvation. The wicked man is confounded by his fault, corrected by penance, so that, corrected, he may be clothed in justice, and justified, may obtain the grace of the just Saviour. So Augustine, interceding, prevailed with victory; he wrested a blessing with Jacob, propitiation with Moses, and as victor brought back again to the wretch the health that had been taken away by the Lord. The man, restored entirely in walking, speech and hearing, ceases thereafter to be led by another's help, ceases to speak with his fingers; others too unlearn the signs they were taught in order to communicate with the deaf man; and made sounder in mind too, he desists from his former windiness [which is more useful than bodily health], namely through the teaching, rebuke, prayer and salvation of father Augustine.
CHAPTER V.
Saint Livinus baptised and instructed. The death and burial of Saint Augustine.

48. Now, among so many marks of miracles, who could worthily set forth the praises of so great a teacher, through whom not only the wilder take up the sweet yoke of Christ, but even holy men, powerful in signs, come to him by a wondrous way to be taught, even at an angel's prompting? The matter is not to be committed to the narrowness of a chapter, but to be set out in plain and clear language. We read in the life of the most blessed bishop and martyr Livinus, written on the trustworthy testimony of his holy companions, how Augustine himself, that most faithful steward of the Lord's affairs, came, out of concern for the salvation of all, to the devout king of Scotia, Colomannus, and baptised blessed Livinus, then a boy, together with the holy bishop Monalchius, and how the king and queen and the nobles of the kingdom received him from the font. Then, moreover, a column of solar brightness shone upon the baptised boy before all, and in the brightness a golden right hand, gleaming brighter than the sun, appeared and three times blessed the boy with the sign of the cross; and a heavenly voice sounded in these words: "Beloved of God and men, whose memory is in blessing." At this the illustrious Augustine glorified the Lord, and gave all an example of glorifying him. Meanwhile that youth, growing in holiness of life, his godson in both age and merit, was so beloved by the king and by all that they tried with wondrous affection and with entreaties to keep him back. As he feared the nets of the world and was anxiously wavering over this, an angel of light shone upon him and, greeting him by his own name, said: "Hail, brother Livinus, cease to be troubled, and hear how you are to be consoled. Go from here to Augustine, bishop of the English, and receive from him instruction in the whole of holy discipline, through whom, with God advancing you, you may attain the summit of virtues." But the confessor of the Lord, hastening to obey the angelic commands, having sought the king's leave and broken the restraints of his supporters like spiders' webs, went of his own accord with three blessed disciples, Foillan, Helias and Kilian [who also became renowned as most reliable authors in describing his deeds], to the sea, so that he might sail across to his most longed-for father Augustine. But an angel of the Lord met him on the way, with youthful beauty, shining face, graceful in his step, sweet in his speech: "Take courage, brother," he said, "for the Lord has sent me to you as guide and inseparable guardian on all your way. Only follow me without hesitation, for with the Lord's favour I will bring you with prosperous success to that teacher of your advancement whom you seek." So the prudent Livinus, recognising that the Spirit of truth was saying this to him, follows him confidently as he goes before, with the disciples mentioned, and together they cross that great and wide sea with dry feet. And it seemed both to the most holy Livinus and to his blessed companions, throughout that whole journey in which they trod on foot the waves of the vast flood as if it were solid ground, that they were passing through meadows or green fields, blooming with roses and lilies and every most beautiful variety of herbs and flowers. And when the starry guide had happily set his followers down on a safe shore, he returned to heaven before their eyes with unspeakable radiance and a broad flash of light, so that by this splendour he seemed to say: "Hasten, sons of light, to follow me here, scorning the darkness of the world." Who, then, doubts that these so flowery and shining miracles are to be ascribed to, or shared with, the merits of the glorious Augustine, so that for those seeking Augustine the wave grew green, the sea flowered, the flood bloomed, and the very abyss beneath the feet of those seeking the evangelist of peace showed itself as a solid field? So the longing Livinus came, with the three confessors of the Holy Trinity named before, to the longed-for father Augustine; he came under an angel's guidance as if to another angel, from a flowery journey to a flower-bearing paradise, from the way of the sea to a honey-flowing spring, from ruinous wealth to the treasurer of incorruptible riches, who might bring forth for him from the chamber of the true King the infinite abundance of things and the unfading beauty of all forms. O what festive joy arose for so exalted a teacher of saints, when he received such a disciple destined for him by God, whom he had foreknown by the Holy Spirit would come, and who was worthy to be the master of others! But the noble nature of Livinus prefers to learn humbly from one so divinely inspired what he would afterwards teach confidently. He hears him who set his mouth in heaven discoursing with angelic mouth on the infinite and glorious multitude of the heavenly powers, on the most excellent hierarchy of apostolic eminence, on the countless army and triumphal palm of the martyrs, on the most radiant crown of confessors and virgins; that all the suffering of the world is not worthy to be compared with such great rewards; that nothing can be compared, nothing valued, against that beauty; that toward that dignity, toward that unfailing festival and joys, one must now run with every kind of labour, with every fragrance of virtues. Toward that prize of everlasting beatitude he led his most eager emulator through all the flower-gardens of the sacred Scriptures; he opened to him the treasuries and storerooms of Christ and the Church, in the delights and pleasures of the Lord's treasures and of life-breathing spices, in the everlasting love and brightness of the saints. With these and very many other exhortations the renowned general of the Lord's camp armed Christ's most valiant athlete, and inflamed him, already most ardent; and now, according to the promise of the angel who had gone before as guide, he raised him to the perfection of apostolic life, so that he might also attain the palm of martyrdom. And so, having kept him with him for five years and three months, and advanced him in all holiness by most holy examples and instruction, young in age but aged in religious maturity, he at last consecrates him a priest most chosen for Christ. At the ordination of his beloved disciple the most generous catechist also gives him a most sweet pledge and memorial of his perpetual love, namely a purple chasuble, foretelling his glorious martyrdom, bordered with gold and gems like his merits; he adds a stole and an *orarium* [a kind of stole or neck-cloth], likewise insignia adorned with gold and with stars of precious gems. And now, having invoked every good upon him, and the mutual support of prayers, not without mutual tears, he sends him back, with his holy companions mentioned before, to his king and people as their most longed-for teacher. In short, as bees seek the honey-flowing flower, and as deer the spring of water, so from every side they sought Augustine as he made heavenly honey.

49. There was a certain old man who asserted that his grandfather had been baptised by Saint Augustine, and that this grandfather had told it to his father, and his father to him, in this way. “When I was,” he said, “a young lad, and had seen the crowds of peoples running together to that new and unheard-of first teacher of our salvation, Augustine, as if to some angel, I, for whom vanity was a crown, folly a joy, and jokes delights, with a wonderful dullness of sense mocked everything as if it were phantoms; and in my great foolishness I believed that everyone was in error except me and my fellow-errants. But when I heard that he healed all the bodies of the sick and dying, in my unbelief I guffawed with greater madness. At length I conceived a trick in my wantonness, and like a windbag I came to see him as if he were a cheat, or to hear him as a babbler; for this purpose, namely, that I might snatch some trick from his mouth or his healing, by which I could raise a laugh among those like me. And when I had plunged into the pressing crowd, like a plotter and a petty thief, and had marked with my eyes his fatherly and reverend gaze, at once I froze, confounded with enormous terror, so that some divine reproof in him seemed to be indignant at my impurity. But he, full of the holy Spirit of God (as has been made clear so far), looked at me, whom he had never seen, as if I were very well known to him; and sending a servant, saying, ‘Bring that young man to me,’ he ordered me to be brought to him from the midst of the people. Then indeed, considering more deeply that I had become known to him without anyone pointing me out, I trembled with such amazement as if I had seen with drawn sword the investigator and punisher of my crime. At once I fled for refuge to the mercy of so great a prophet, and, prostrating myself, clasped his holy feet. There I let out all the swelling of my windiness like a pricked bladder, I vomited up all the filth of my loose levity, I gave myself wholly to the precepts and teachings of so kind a father. He, having gently rebuked and instructed me, embraced me in fatherly arms, baptised me as a believer in Christ, and blessed me into sons of lilies, from a long-extended life.” These things and twice as many more the old man aforesaid, heard from his grandfather by his father and told to him by his father, set before his hearers with an assertion of good faith, as if known from another age. He also made known the form of blessed Augustine himself, as conveyed to him by his parents, and his patrician bearing: a tall and lofty stature, so that he stood above the people from the shoulders up, and displayed Saul in tallness, not in fierceness. His face was lovable and reverend; his forehead, with the hair parted in the middle, stood out windowed between its columns. But the signs and healings which he constantly performed among the people who thronged to him and the gathering of the sick, he declared no one could relate or count. It was remembered that he always travelled the provinces on foot with apostolic devotion, often barefoot, and had drawn onto his soles the calluses of the knees of James, the brother of the Lord; and he asserted that many of his holy companions also were accustomed either to imitate or to equal the same virtues. Hence, therefore, since charity believes all things that are probable, and since we readily believe what we love, but what we do not believe we prove that we hate or despise, let the sons of love, and not strangers, consider that the things which the saints did in their life could have come, by God making them known, to the notice of the holy Scriptures, either through writings, or through long-lived elders, or through report (which is the law of history) handed down from generation to generation; and that it is no wrong to believe such things and of such kind. Now, after the rivers and the beasts driven back, let us unfold the victory of glorious Augustine.

50. Long since, that dweller on high, struck by that wound of heavenly love which is strong as death, shrank from all earthly delights as harms to life, and from worldly glory as from chains, as from prison-houses, as from punishments; and yet [he thought] it would be sweet to suffer all these things, even death itself, for the Saviour. And so, bound to the earth by his body alone, or rather held only by fatherly care for begetting and forming lilies for God, for the rest he dwelt wholly in that eternal homeland; with his whole mind, his whole soul, with constant and violent urgency he reached for heavenly things. What incense of prayers, what laments of holy desires, what unutterable sighs he sent to heaven! “Who,” he says, “will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly and be at rest?” and, “When shall I come and appear before the face of my God? My soul longed and fainted for the courts of the Lord.” So with restless cries he came before the face of the Lord, and did violence to heaven, asking with frequent knocking to be admitted, desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ. At length, understanding from the answer of the Holy Spirit that his desire had been heard, that he should come to him who is desired by all the upright of heart, he began with a parent’s heart to fear anxiously that after him the milk-fed infancy of the Church, born or being born, bereaved of its shepherd, would be torn apart by the invasion of wolves. Hence, as the Lord said to him in spirit, “Anoint this man for me as chosen priest,” he resolved with clear-sighted mind and heavenly prompting that blessed Laurence, a man of apostolic holiness, renowned for apostolic signs, and foremost of his companions, should be ordained in his place. He refers this to the clergy, to the king, to the people: it pleases all, all approve, together they bless and ask for it. And so, with the king and the people flocking together rejoicing immensely, he ordains Laurence as his successor with all solemn joy, as once Peter, the prince of the apostles, [ordained] Clement, namely because of the aforesaid need of new instruction; yet this example ought not to be presumed upon by anyone hereafter. No one did this rightly after Peter; let no one do it improperly after Augustine. For there is one Christ, one Church, one bishop, and the one and the unity is not divided. So he sends the consecrated man, most ready for everything, as Paul sent Timothy, into the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, that he might run about, hasten, press on in season and out of season, reprove, entreat, in all patience and teaching. He himself, a contemplative beholder, as a refugee from the oppressive world, as a sparrow alone on the roof, rejoiced greatly, the bonds of things broken, to fly up to the Lord on the wings of eternal love, to rest in the best part of Mary, to be free for God alone, to stand before the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, and to feed on his everlasting sweetness. Then at last he believed that he lived and reigned, then first that he had begun to serve God. Yet he never failed to increase the Lord’s gains, in gathering peoples together and kings themselves to serve the Lord: nowhere was he absent where divine business required. Now, like an eagle, he flew to the heights; now, when the Lord’s [flock] required it, he revisited the pastures below.

51. Why does my speech, with long evasion, dread to tell of his departure from this present light?
