At length the most victorious champion of the Lord, having run the course of life in all holiness and perfection of merits, reached the prize and the long-desired rewards of the eternal kingdom. Now, as the Lord knocked through sickness, he opened to him, with unutterable rejoicing and a fragrant sacrifice of thanksgiving. Then with the great-hearted affection of fatherly love he exhorted king and princes as well as clergy and people to serve the Lord in fear; and, having cast off the filth of demonic sacrifices, to persevere immovably in the faith of Christ divinely handed down to them through him; and to cleave to the one living and true God with faith and everlasting love; and diligently to observe his commandments through the anointed bishop and the Lord’s ministers. So the end of worldly storms came, and the dawn of eternal joys shone forth: and having blessed the king, and confirmed in Christ the Church, the firstborn of his begetting, leaving to all pledges of everlasting love and teachings of the blessed life, amid tearful throngs of his holy companions and disciples, with blessed Laurence standing by with a crowd of people, he laid down the burden of the flesh and was taken up into heaven, with the triumph and glory of the heavenly powers, with the inestimable meeting and welcome of all, and with everlasting joy. O with what solemnity was the whole of heaven then adorned and crowned, at the arrival of so illustrious a citizen! The heavenly squadrons surround the palm-bearing victor, the apostles invite their apostolic companion to their seats, the purple-clad camp of the martyrs ring round their martyr standard-bearer, the shining ranks of confessors and the venerable throng of priests embrace the distinguished hierarch, the white-robed choirs of virgins sing with sweet hymns to their virgin leader; and, to speak in mortal fashion of those unutterable mysteries of heavenly harmonies, then that great Jerusalem, the city of the great King, saw at once its peoples and tribes, together resounding in Augustine’s triumph with unwearied thanks and praises to the Lord. Let all of us, the lowest, though praisers as unworthy as unequal, follow them as we can, not with funeral laments but with these triumphal songs: You reign, Augustine, more exalted in name and dignity than the age of Augustus, you who enlarged the commonwealth of Christ, and added Britain to the Roman Church better than Caesar Augustus added Alexandria to Roman wealth. Kings and princes and the senate of the English, and the crowd of nations, accompany you into heaven; angels and archangels lead you in triumph, thrones and dominions receive you, the King of kings crowns you.

52. The most precious pearl of his body the most excellently chosen Laurence, after a magnificent dedication had been held, together with the most devout King Æthelberht and the peoples of England flocking together, laid to rest in that very apostolic and royal monastery which he himself, with God as its author, had founded, namely in the northern side-chapel of that same sacred hall, where he stored it up as a treasure deposited in eternal memory of the heavenly kingdom.

53. But while we hasten to finish so holy a history, we are still stubbornly held, both by the gracious sweetness of this angelic place and by the infinite gift of the love of the saints, which satisfies the full and fills those who long for it, to recall sweetly how the heavenly tombs of so many of the first teachers of Britain, or rather of so many angels of God, filled that side-chapel. In these it should be noted with gratitude what noble offspring Rome, the universal mother, brought forth to be fathers and instructors to the very British Ocean: and while one love bound them together in one chamber, many nations held them as their own patrons, each distinguished separately and set over them with his own rays. Of these the most excellent Augustine made Laurence, the dedicator of this church, his successor (as was shown above); he ordained Mellitus bishop of London and Justus bishop of the church of Rochester; and these, after [Laurence], exiled for Christ's sake, Mellitus received as third and Justus as fourth successor. To these was joined as fifth Honorius, himself also a seemly honour of Roman training. Sixth in order was Deusdedit, but the first flower of the English people, who passed into the enrolment of the Roman fathers: the Roman foundations of Dorobernia had nothing more pleasing than these first fruits from England. Seventh also, Theodore, an outstanding follower of Roman excellence, was buried with the kindly Augustine at his right side, with only one wall of the monastery's body standing between them, because the side-chapel, not yet enlarged, could not take them all: when it was later widened, there was joined to these holy companions Adrian, to be loved by all ages, the most gentle abbot of the same monastery; who, having been chosen by the apostolic lord at Rome as archbishop of Dorobernia, brought the blessed Theodore himself in his place, and with him made the English teachable by God in both Greek and Latin learning. Likewise the whitest lily from the English, Mildred, the royal virgin of Christ, most pleasingly lights up with her whiteness the splendid adornments of such great fathers. The author of all these, therefore, the most blessed Pope Gregory, holding the central altar as a patrician throne, and guarding the very side-chapel dedicated to God, embraces with eternal love not so much the remains of those buried together as the dining-couches of those feasting together: but before all he binds Augustine to himself, as the chief of his institution, the firstborn of his labour, first both in life and in rank. The other sons too, who are the ecclesiastical first parents of England, recline like young olive shoots around his table. On the original tomb of the most pre-eminent Augustine an epitaph is written of this kind: Here rests the lord Augustine, first archbishop of Dorobernia, who, sent here long ago by the blessed Gregory, pontiff of the city of Rome, and supported by God with the working of miracles, led King Æthelberht and his people from the worship of idols to the faith of Christ, and, having completed in peace the days of his office, died on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, in the reign of the same king. About these seven first pillars of the English church, too, hewn from the Tarpeian rock of Rome, these verses are added: Their inscriptions, written above in their order, are these: Of the countless signs which the blessed Augustine has shown, in answer to the faith of those who ask, in this dormitory of his rest or among any peoples or places, the following little book will relate a number which have been proved before the eyes of the faithful, God guiding us in his truth, who, reigning through all ages, always shows himself wonderful in his saints. (This little book can be read in the Bollandists, vol. V of May, p. 862.)

Seven primates and first fathers have the English, seven rulers and seven plough-stars through the sky; they are seven stars, the floor of one cell holds them; seven cisterns of life, and seven lamps; and seven palms of the kingdom, and seven crowns. Indeed, the seven eyes with which Christ sees this world, as the world runs through the ages in seven days.
The leader Augustine excels, first in order; laurelled and pure, second in Laurence's see; third is pleasing Mellitus, honey-laden; fourth is present Justus, giving sweet tastes in his name.
Fifth, Honorius stands forth, the strength and honour of the Church;

Deusdedit is sixth, to whom Christ gives his gifts. Theodore, seventh, brings the kindly sabbath close by. By these seven leaders England flourishes, and by as many days. An eighth is added, Adrian, leader of monks. Mildred, star of the English, brings back her honey. Eight fathers are of Rome; the rest, born of the English, accompany them in honour, joined to them by merits. From here the way of the Gospel flows in divine streams: these are Brihtwald, Tatwine, and you, Nothelm, and now Berta, imitating the first fathers and chiefs; so many together encircle the front of the Church with piety.
